detail.abstract:
Parts I to VIII built a governance architecture piece by piece. Part I separated the engine that proposes from the engine that verifies, and put a hardware veto at the point of actuation. Part II turned this into standards, conformance tests and device-class profiles. Part III drew the line between cloud and edge. Part IV made verified results into assets. Parts V and VI placed AI in society as a governed non-person. Part VIII showed that sovereign states can adopt one standard without trusting each other.

This part adds no new principle or mechanism. It carries the cloud–edge principle of Part III from theory to the ground and asks two practical questions. How should the work of an AI system be split between the cloud and the edge? And how are the existing pieces of governance declared, assembled and verified on a real device, in any industry, at any scale, so that the result is the same machine every time? Our answer is a deployment blueprint in two halves. The first half is the split. The cloud may propose, but verification and the actuation veto stay at the sovereign edge, and the share of each task that must run locally is set by five factors: data sovereignty, irreversibility, verification and domain collaboration, model control, and ecosystem resilience. Four doctrines and the Five Verification Anchors of Part III make the split auditable. The second half is governance. Every governed deployment has two parts. The first is an invariant core: a small set of rules, enforced in hardware at the point where a command becomes a physical act, that is the same on every device. The second is a set of five settings that change from one deployment to the next. We call them dials. Four already exist in the series: the kind of device, the size of the deployment, an eight-point configuration checklist, and the kind of reasoning allowed. The fifth is new. We call it the anchor binding. It states what the gate measures, under which conditions, against which limit, and where the device rests when the check fails. Section 1.4 explains each idea in plain words, and Appendix IX-C defines every term, so the part can be read on its own.

The part makes three contributions. First, it fills the one empty column of the device-class table of Part II: an anchor binding for each class, and a rule for placing new domains. Second, it tests the pattern against the safety mechanisms that industries already use, from vehicles and robots to aircraft and medical devices. All of them have an anchor and a safe state; none of them handles a proposer that cannot be analysed, can be replaced over the network, and may run under another state. Third, it shows that the same shape holds at three scales: a device, an estate of many devices, and a group of sovereigns that do not trust each other. These three results are carried by one normative standard, ISO-GOS-0: Basis of Governance and Edge Integration, which binds the static standards (ISO-GOS-1/2/3) and the dynamic series (4001–4004) at the edge. We close with the evidence that would refute these claims. Before the blueprint, the part turns the twelve systemic risks of AI named in Part V into twelve concrete scenarios at the edge. After it, the part sets out an adoption path of six levels, AL-0 to AL-5, of which the first three need no gate hardware.

detail.abstract: The Federal Reserve sets its interest rate target exclusively in multiples of 25 basis points. We argue that this discretization affects expectations management: most forecasters predict Fed decisions exactly, but any surprises are necessarily large and may require active recalibration of expectations. We show that 99.6% of analyst forecasts of the Fed's target rate are multiples of 25 basis points and that disagreement almost always reduces to a choice between two adjacent grid points. When the share of wrong analyst forecasts is higher by one standard deviation, equity returns on the next FOMC announcement day are 35 basis points higher and VIX declines are steeper, with both effects concentrated in the pre-announcement period. A high share of wrong forecasts also amplifies the even-week FOMC cycle pattern for both equity returns and VIX changes, but does not predict changes in fed funds futures prices or Treasury yields. After surprises, public communications by Fed officials do not increase, but FOMC transcripts show that the Committee discusses financial market reactions more extensively at the following meeting. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that, after surprising markets, Fed officials engage in informal communication that reduces market uncertainty without affecting the yield curve.

detail.abstract: Better predictions and broader allocation flexibility create complementary economic value. I measure their returns in 25 Chicago food-inspection queues from 2013 to 2026, covering 27,637 inspections and 6,473 failures. Predictions use pre-origin information; comparisons hold observed outcomes and daily inspection slots fixed. Boosting advances failure discovery by 5.61 days and reaches the historical first-month discovery target with 25.3% fewer inspection slots. A crossed comparison within logistic regression separates information from allocation flexibility. Adding establishment and location information with ZIP-specific workloads fixed improves discovery timing by 0.03 days. Expanding allocation citywide with history scores fixed adds 1.17 days. Improving both adds 2.21 days, including a 1.01-day interaction with a 95% paired interval of 0.25 to 1.73 days. Under boosting, within-ZIP prioritisation accounts for 451 additional firstmonth discoveries and citywide flexibility adds another 390. Prediction's value depends on the decisions it can change. Information and the organisation of allocation jointly determine the economic return to algorithms.

detail.abstract: Conglomerate mergers are commonly regarded as harmless. detail.abstract:
Policymakers tend to treat a handful of frontier labs as the whole of AI. We map what is being built outside them. Working layer by layer from hardware to governance, we document nearly 30 systems, institutions, and standards that are already running. We draw on 36 interviews conducted between April and August 2026 and on case studies written by practitioners at OpenMined, the Ethereum Foundation, and Civic AI.

Chip manufacturing and frontier-scale training remain concentrated, but every other layer has working alternatives. Community data licenses, such as Te Hiku Media’s guardianship license for Māori speech data, let the people who contributed the data set the terms of its use. Ai2 releases the training data and code for its OLMo models along with the weights. Small models built for one language can match much larger ones on the tasks their communities need, as Lelapa AI’s InkubaLM does for five African languages. At the inference layer, privacy-preserving infrastructure lets a regulator or outside researcher audit a model without holding its weights or data, an approach OpenMined has piloted with Anthropic and the UK AI Security Institute. Most of these systems sit outside the safety debate about frontier models, because a bounded system built for one community does not carry a frontier model’s catastrophic risk. The alternatives also help with the risks that remain around open frontier weights and AI agents by supplying outside verification and the identity infrastructure agents need.

Earlier general-purpose technologies, including the railroad and the telephone, went through periods of both concentration and decentralization. Finance and public policy shaped which way they went. The alternatives that could keep AI plural already exist, so concentration need not be its final stage either. We do not treat concentration as a moral failure or argue that every system must be decentralized, and we do not make the case for open frontier weights.

detail.abstract:
Permissioned Distributed ledger technology (DLT) systems are being developed for shared financial market infrastructures (FMIs) to reduce reconciliation needs and enable pro-grammable, atomic settlement. Many permissioned systems use Proof-of-Authority (PoA) or related authority-based mechanisms, which assign transaction ordering, inclusion, and
finality to a restricted set of validators. Using comparative institutional analysis, this paper examines how validators’ competitive position affects the ability of such a system to function as shared infrastructure. We argue that the institutional viability of authority-based consensus depends not only on technical performance, but also on the identity, mandate,
and incentives of the authorized validators. With a single competing validator, residual ordering discretion creates dependence on a rival and can discourage participation. Multi-validator PoA distributes control, but shifts economically contested decisions into collective governance among competitors. Operational restrictions and institutional controls can ad-dress particular conflicts; their effectiveness depends on the allocation and enforceability of decision rights. Validator identity alone therefore does not determine suitability as shared infrastructure. The paper thus identifies validators’ competitive position as a key determinant of whether a shared DLT system can function as FMI.

Findings-In line with our proposed framework, FLE digital integration enhances FLE bricolage, and this relationship is moderated by manager intellectual stimulation. Furthermore, FLE bricolage increases adaptive selling and job performance. Practical implications-Organizations should invest in promoting the adoption of digital technologies among FLEs to enhance employee bricolage. Organizations should also train their managers to display intellectually stimulating behaviors to enhance the effects of digital technologies among their frontlines. Originality/value-Our research provides novel insights by identifying digital integration and manager intellectual stimulation as critical drivers of FLE bricolage. Furthermore, FLE bricolage enhances FLE performance.

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Many sellers reprice against rivals' prices, but the rival price they use is often inexact: matching rival offers to a seller's products is error-prone when products have many variants. We show how the precision of that price moves prices when firms adapt to data rather than compute equilibria. 
   
Methodology/results: In a duopoly with private, correlated costs and an offline channel, we characterize where two adaptive pricing processes stop. A model-based firm regresses its sales on its price and the rival price it observes. Its own-price slope estimate is biased by the unseen part of the rival's price, which moves with the firm's own price through correlated costs and the rival's response. The bias equals the cross-price demand slope times the cost correlation when the observed price is uninformative. As precision rises, the rival responds more while the firm controls for more of the rival's price, so the bias can rise. A first improvement from an uninformative price raises the mean price whenever the cost correlation is below a threshold set by competition intensity. Full precision removes the bias. During learning, a common drift in both prices adds to the bias, prices can overshoot, and moderate precision removes most of the overshoot. When model-based firms choose their precision, at our benchmark no equilibrium has both at full precision: exact rival prices are optimal against an uninformed rival but not against an exactly informed one. A rule-tuning firm, which never re-estimates its price sensitivity, keeps its mean price at every precision. With a correct belief, precision only synchronizes prices. A seven-month pharmacy panel documents the information structure and judgment-based repricing. 

Managerial implications: Better rival-price information lowers long-run prices only where sellers re-estimate demand, and from low precision can first raise them. At our benchmark, such sellers' precision choices keep mean prices 1 to 4 percent above the Nash level. Full precision for both would raise consumer surplus and commission revenue at the sellers' expense.

detail.abstract: Legal responses to neurotechnology have converged on two strategies: constitutional recognition of brain-related protections, as in Chile (2021) and Rio Grande do Sul (2023), and the extension of data-protection statutes to a category of "neural data," as in Colorado, California, Connecticut and Montana. This article asks whether either strategy protects the interests that the concept of cognitive liberty identifies, namely the integrity of the processes through which a person forms, holds and revises mental states, and, if not, what legal trigger would. The method is doctrinal and comparative legal analysis of constitutional texts, statutes, a supranational data-protection judgment, the Chilean Supreme Court's 2023 decision in Girardi v. Emotiv, and international soft-law instruments, supplemented by a critical reading of one advocacy-group survey of consumer-device privacy policies. The article develops a distinction between provenance-based and function-based legal triggers. Its authorial argument is that provenance-based definitions, which attach protection to data generated by measuring the nervous system, are under-inclusive, because mental states can be inferred from non-neural signals, and largely silent on modulation, whereas the interests at stake are functional. Drawing on freedom of thought under Article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, on the Court of Justice of the European Union's inference-sensitive reading of special-category data, and on the function-based prohibitions of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the article proposes a two-trigger architecture that preserves a direct-measurement floor while adding context-calibrated protection against mental-state inference and modulation. The proposal is normative, faces serious objections concerning breadth and enforceability, and is accompanied by stated conditions under which it would be weakened or falsified. The contribution is a comparative-doctrinal diagnosis and a reasoned legislative-design argument, not an empirical finding.

detail.abstract:
Background: Peru has substantially reduced child stunting, but national trends may mask unequal progress across socioeconomic groups. We assessed trends in prevalence and wealth-related inequalities among children younger than 5 years from 2010 to 2025 and identified changes over time.

Methods: We analysed 16 annual rounds of Peru’s Demographic and Family Health Survey as a repeated cross-sectional study. We estimated national and wealth-quintile prevalence, absolute and relative gaps, the Slope Index of Inequality (SII), and the Erreygers Concentration Index (CIxE). Bayesian segmented regression identified change points; frequentist Joinpoint models assessed sensitivity.

Findings: National prevalence decreased from 23·3% in 2010 to 12·1% in 2025; from 44·0% to 22·7% in the poorest quintile and from 5·4% to 3·4% in the richest. The absolute gap decreased from 38·7 to 19·3 percentage points; the relative gap from 8·22 to 6·67; the SII from −50·6 to −27·2 percentage points; and the CIxE from −0·340 to −0·174. National prevalence declined by 8·8% annually until approximately 2016, after which the decline slowed until approximately 2021. Thereafter, prevalence showed a slight, statistically non-significant increase of 0·8% annually. Inequalities decreased throughout the study period, more rapidly before approximately 2016 than afterwards. Frequentist analyses were concordant.

Interpretation: Peru achieved substantial reductions in child stunting and wealth-related inequalities. However, recent slowing and the persistent concentration of stunting among lower-wealth households indicate the need to combine reductions in national prevalence with explicit actions and targets to progressively narrow wealth-related gaps.

detail.abstract:
Background: Child stunting has declined unevenly across socioeconomic groups in Peru. We described national prevalence and wealth-half gaps, examined associated characteristics, decomposed wealth-related inequality, assessed changes in contributions over time, and evaluated territorial variation in the leading contributor’s association with stunting.

Methods: We analyzed eight ENDES rounds (2010–2025) among children aged 0–59 months. Stunting was defined as a WHO height-for-age z score below −2. We estimated survey-weighted prevalence by wealth half and adjusted associations. We decomposed wealth-half gaps using Fairlie and Oaxaca–Blinder–Yun, and full-gradient inequality using Wagstaff–van Doorslaer–Watanabe (WVW) and Kessels–Erreygers. Extreme-tertile analyses assessed sensitivity, and contributions were grouped using three WHO frameworks.

Findings: The eight rounds included 135,214 children for descriptive analyses and 123,643 complete cases for association and decomposition. From 2010 to 2025, national prevalence declined from 23·3% to 12·1%, and the lower-versus-upper-half gap from 24·7 to 10·6 percentage points. The Fairlie gap magnitude decreased from 0·218 (95% CI 0·195–0·240) to 0·098 (0·087–0·109), and the WVW index magnitude from 0·300 (0·271–0·328) to 0·157 (0·139–0·174). Observed characteristics explained 72·2% and 69·6% of these measures, respectively, in 2025. Area of residence contributed most (48·9% and 45·7%), followed by basic water and sanitation, maternal stature, and maternal education. Low birthweight and short maternal stature showed the strongest associations. Extreme-tertile analyses showed similar patterns.

Interpretation: Peru reduced child stunting and socioeconomic inequality, but the gap persisted and area of residence contributed most to the explained component. These noncausal findings support sustaining educational and material gains, territorially oriented intersectoral responses, and explicit equity monitoring.

detail.abstract: In many developing economies, minimum wages do not merely set a floor for formal earnings; they also anchor social security contributions, turning minimum wage reforms into mechanical increases in the fixed cost of formal employment. This paper combines evidence from workers and firms to estimate how these minimum contribution requirements reshape labor market duality and inequality. Exploiting legislative reforms to minimum wages and statutory contribution rates across Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru (2006-2024), I construct a continuous "contribution bite" that varies across demographic cells and across firms, and combine harmonized household and firm microdata to identify its causal impact. On the worker margin, a 1% increase in a group's exposure to the contribution floor raises the informal employment share by 0.92%. Higher exposure also compresses earnings dispersion within both the formal and informal sectors, consistent with a lighthouse effect on informal wages. On the firm margin, a 1% increase in a firm's exposure reduces formal employment by 3.4% and total sales by 7.3%. A worker-flow identity reconciles the two: roughly half of the formal job losses reappear as informal employment in the household data. Together, the findings show that when social protection is tied to the minimum wage, it inadvertently excludes vulnerable workers and firms from the formal sector.

detail.abstract: We study how frictions impact haircut setting in repo markets. Using transaction-level supervisory data and exploiting the 2021 introduction of the binding leverage ratio requirement, we show that three frictions jointly shape haircuts in the bilateral dealer-to-client segment: dealer balance sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options. In collateral-driven repos, binding leverage constraints and broader client outside options both raise haircuts, while higher convenience yields push them down. In funding-driven trades, the leverage constraint has no effect, higher convenience yields raise haircuts through the rehypothecation channel, and broader client outside options lower them. We rationalise these patterns in a bilateral bargaining model with periodic haircut renegotiation. Consistent with the model, constrained dealers exhibit higher repo-rate volatility and weaker pass-through of ECB policy rate changes in the collateral-driven segment. Post-crisis bank regulation thus carries potential unintended consequences for repo market functioning and the transmission of monetary policy.

detail.abstract:
Background: Oesophageal squamous‑cell carcinoma (ESCC) imposes a heavy disease burden within the Western‑Pacific region, where neoadjuvant therapy followed by surgery is widely implemented. Preoperative identification of pathological complete response (pCR) is critical to guide organ‑preserving strategies and avoid unnecessary oesophagectomy. Radiomics‑based machine learning (ML) models hold potential for this task, yet available evidence is geographically clustered and the relative diagnostic performance across different ML algorithms remains unclear. We aimed to compare the diagnostic accuracy of ML models for predicting pCR using a Bayesian diagnostic network meta‑analysis.

Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Scopus, ProQuest, and Web of Science up to Sep 30, 2026. Eligible studies enrolled histologically confirmed ESCC patients receiving neoadjuvant therapy, used postoperative pathology as reference standard, and evaluated ≥3 ML models. We fitted bivariate random-effects models to calculate pooled sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve. Bivariate random-effects models were used to pool sensitivity, specificity and SROC AUC. Bayesian hierarchical network meta-analysis calculated SUCRA for model ranking. We assessed reporting quality (TRIPOD+AI), radiomics methodology (RQS 2.0), risk of bias (PROBAST+AI), and publication bias (Deeks’ funnel test). This review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261520575).

Findings: 12 eligible studies were included. Seven ML algorithms were assessed in internal validation datasets and five in external validation. In internal validation, the Extra‑Trees model yielded an AUC of 0.842 (95%CI 0.766-0.918; sensitivity 84.6%, specificity 72.4%). In external validation, Random Forest achieved an AUC of 0.829 (95%CI 0.756-0.902; sensitivity 69.3%, specificity 80.6%) and Extra‑Trees an AUC of 0.818 (95%CI 0.738-0.898; sensitivity 79.1%, specificity 74.7%). Most included studies had a high risk of bias and incomplete reporting; 75% of training cohorts had an events-per-variable ratio below 10, raising substantial concerns of model overfitting.

Interpretation: ML models yield moderate‑to‑good discriminative performance for preoperative pCR prediction in ESCC. Observations from retrospective datasets indicated relatively stable discriminative results for Extra Trees and Random Forest across internal and external validation settings. Nevertheless, evidence certainty remains limited by methodological shortcomings, pronounced geographic clustering of study cohorts within the Western-Pacific region, and scarce geographically‑independent external validation. Current models are not ready to alter routine clinical practice. Standardised prospective multicentre validation, including calibration assessment and clinical impact studies, is required before clinical adoption.

detail.abstract: Holding limits are a central design feature of proposed retail central bank digital currencies (CBDC). While such limits mechanically prevent individuals from exceeding a maximum balance, they may also generate behavioral responses whose directions are a priori unclear. We conducted an incentivized online experiment with participants from four euro-area countries, exogenously varying the presence and level of a holding limit to causally separate direct mechanical effects from behavioral effects. We find that behavioral responses increase holdings of the means of payment subject to the holding limit, consistent with an attraction effect. This effect is material only when the limit is high enough. Enabling reverse waterfall —automatic conversion into this limited means of payment— increases adoption while reducing holdings. These results suggest that combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms can support CBDC use while containing holdings, thereby helping to mitigate potential financial stability risks.

detail.abstract:
Background: Routine childhood immunisation fell during the COVID-19 pandemic. Global averages now suggest a rebound. It is less clear whether each country regained its own pre-2020 path for DTP3, the primary indicator.

Methods: We analysed WHO–UNICEF coverage for 193 countries, 2015–2024 (1,929 country-years). DTP3 was the primary outcome; MCV1 and HepB3 were secondary. A segmented panel model with country fixed effects estimated the gap between fitted coverage and the extended pre-2020 trend. Standard errors were clustered by country. Children without DTP3 were births multiplied by the uncovered share. A five-class rule grouped countries against 2019. An empirical-Bayes “recovery clock” described current pace. Rolling-origin back-tests chose the 2030 forecast.

Findings: Births-weighted DTP3 coverage was 86.2% in 2019, 81.4% in 2021 and 84.5% in 2024. Children without DTP3 rose from 19.06 million to 24.74 million, then fell to 20.53 million. In 2024, DTP3 was 2.40 points below the 2015–2019 trend (95% CI −4.30 to −0.51). Longer baselines gave smaller gaps (−1.11 to −1.56 points). Overall, 108 of 192 countries (56.2%) remained below 2019 coverage. Unlike previous studies, we back-tested 2030 forecasts; a no-change forecast was most accurate (5-year error 4.91 points vs 6.58 for trends). Under it, an expected 76.0 of these countries (95% UI 67–85) would remain below 2019 in 2030; across methods, 70.6–76.0. With births held at 2024 levels, 21.85 million children would lack DTP3 in 2030. A deeper 2020–2021 drop was associated with non-recovery (OR per SD 2.81, 95% CI 1.71 to 4.61).

Interpretation: Global rebound figures hide incomplete and, for most lagging countries, stalled recovery. These 2030 figures are model-dependent scenarios, but every method suggests most lagging countries will not regain 2019 without faster catch-up.

detail.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome that imposes a substantial burden on global healthcare systems. While artificial intelligence models have shown promise for early sepsis detection, the majority rely on continuous time-series data from intensive care units, limiting their applicability to emergency department (ED) settings where data are typically single-time, incomplete, and irregularly collected. This study presents a comprehensive framework for sepsis prediction using snapshot clinical data obtained at the point of initial patient admission. A retrospective dataset of 237 patients, labeled according to Sepsis-3 criteria, was used. Three feature subsets of increasing dimensionality were constructed based on discriminative power (Set 1: Minimalist with 5 features, Set 2: Balanced with 10, Set 3: Comprehensive with 21), and four imputation strategies were applied: Mean, Median, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and a proposed Missing Gaussian Process (MGP) method that preserves the covariance structure between clinical variables. These combinations were evaluated across six classifiers comprising three classical machine learning models (Random Forest, SVM, XGBoost) and three deep learning architectures (CNN, LSTM, Attention). The MGP method achieved the lowest imputation error (RMSE: 32,270.65; R2: 0.83) and, when paired with tree-based classifiers, yielded an AUROC of 1.00 across all feature sets. In contrast, deep learning models exhibited marked performance degradation as dimensionality increased, particularly under univariate imputation. These results demonstrate that MGP-enhanced ensemble models constitute the most robust approach for ED-based sepsis prediction and that probabilistic imputation is critical for maintaining data integrity in incomplete clinical datasets.

detail.abstract: Administrative guidance can secure compliance before its recipient has a decision to challenge. In the inaugural issue of the Pacific Rim Law & Policy Journal, Dan Fenno Henderson approached that problem through a distinction between Western justiciable law and Chinese and Japanese disciplinary ordering. His distinction conflates the availability of independent judicial review with the existence of legal constraints within other institutions. The Shanghai Mixed Court's divided jurisdiction, disputes over the interpretation of Qing judgments, and Henderson's own account of Tokugawa jurisprudence permit a more discriminating comparison. In contemporary Japanese, Chinese, and American administrative law, access to a remedy depends on the stage at which officials apply a standard and the form their intervention takes. I propose a duty of justification when an authority makes refusal of guidance a material reason for imposing or procuring a disadvantage. Under this principle of reviewable escalation, the recipient could challenge both the asserted duty and the consequence of its alleged breach. Reconsideration would include lawful alternatives, with participation available to people whose legally protected interests an accommodation threatens. Japan's 2025 AI Act provides the application: its cooperation duty requires an account of what an operator owes, while any adverse response requires authority of its own.

detail.abstract: Self-reported data and national registers are commonly used in research to identify hip fractures, but both have known limitations in terms of accuracy and completeness. Self-reported data are susceptible to recall bias, underreporting, and inconsistent accuracy. For patient data and registers, difficulties in identifying true native hip fractures arise from atypical presentations, misclassifications, and clinically suspected cases lacking radiological confirmation. They also may erroneously duplicate hip fractures in cases of continued care or unrelated events on patients who previously sustained a hip fracture. This study investigates the longitudinal agreement and reliability of recorded hip fracture events across self-reports, patient medical records, and the national health register over a 35-year period. Data were cross-checked to identify all hip fractures between 1989 and 2023 in the Kuopio Osteoporosis Risk Factor and Prevention Study and Kuopio Fall Prevention Study, encompassing 16,726 postmenopausal women. A gold standard was established by manually validating all confirmed hip fractures across these sources. During the follow-up, 1,454 native hip fractures were verified. Self-reported data demonstrated substantial underreporting with a low crude sensitivity of 22.0% (adjusted sensitivity 56.5% among responders) but fair agreement (Cohen’s kappa 0.290). In contrast, the national health register was highly accurate, demonstrating 99.8% sensitivity and near-perfect agreement (Cohen’s kappa 0.971). Longitudinal analysis showed a progressive decline in self-report sensitivity as the cohort aged, falling from 45% to 16% over a 30-year period among all participants. Meanwhile, register accuracy remained consistently high throughout the entire follow-up. Surveys offer valuable information, but this long-term validation shows that self-reported hip fractures are limited by low sensitivity that declines significantly with advancing age. The health register maintains high reliability regardless of patient age. For thorough capture of hip fractures in aging populations, multiple data sources should be utilized to mitigate the impact of age-related reporting bias.

detail.abstract: The U.S. mortgage market features substantial geographic heterogeneity in climate risk, while Government-Sponsored Enterprises (GSEs) securitize mortgages at nationally uniform fees. I study how lenders respond to this pricing structure and how these responses shape regional redistribution. Using sea-level-rise (SLR) exposure, I show that lenders price climate risk more strongly for jumbo loans, which are primarily balance-sheet funded, while increasing GSE securitization of conforming loans in more exposed areas. I estimate a structural model of mortgage demand, lender competition, and endogenous funding choice. Under uniform GSE pricing, implicit transfers flow from inland to coastal borrowers, are concentrated among highly exposed borrowers, are regressive across income, and are larger in more competitive markets. Allowing lenders to adjust mortgage rates in equilibrium increases aggregate subsidies by 13.8% to 17.3% relative to a one-to-one pass-through benchmark, with the largest amplification coming from pricing spillovers to jumbo loans. Local SLR-risk pricing eliminates these transfers but substantially reduces mortgage lending and borrower surplus in highly exposed coastal markets, while inducing commercial banks to retain more conforming loans on their balance sheets.

detail.abstract: Optimisation uncertainty-the difficulty of mapping a representation of the decision problem into an action-is particularly consequential in strategic games. It is distinct from the encoding uncertainty studied in the literature, which arises from two inputs: noisy beliefs about others' contributions, and noisy access to one's own preference. We elicit confidence by asking participants how certain they are about their contributions in a repeated, randomly rematched public goods game, and remove or control each source of encoding uncertainty. Confidence does not respond to a treatment removing the first, nor does it rise with repetition as the second would predict, leaving optimisation uncertainty as what remains. From choices and confidence reports we then estimate ideal (full-confidence) and default (zero-confidence) decisions. The ideal, when others do not contribute, is positive for a majority of participants, so contributions are not motivated by confusion alone but also by kindness.

detail.abstract: Lawyers write the rules that price lawyers. Then they call it self-regulation. Advocates Remuneration Order in Kenya sets fees that advocates may not undercut. Section 29 of the Competition Act demands that any professional rule lessening competition first win exemption from the Competition Authority. Section 29(8) adds a prison term for those who ignore it. The High Court has blessed that penalty. The Supreme Court has declined to examine a Sh43.7 million bill that swallowed about 1.5 per cent of a Sh2.9 billion debt. This article reads both decisions together. It argues that the fee floor has two authors, the guild and the state, and that the exemption machinery reaches neither cleanly. It shows a scale that behaves as a ceiling in the taxing room and as a floor in the market. Section 29 was meant to discipline guilds. It has instead disciplined the wrong layer entirely. Poor Kenyans pay for that confusion. The article closes with seven reforms that return price discipline to evidence and legal services to the public.

detail.abstract: Contemporary central bank communication focuses predominantly on delivering forward guidance to specialized audiences, notably financial market analysts and large corporate enterprises. For wage-earning households and small businesses, this orientation leaves a pronounced informational gap. Because non-specialist agents tend to form beliefs through backward-looking, localized price experiences, they often require retrospective explanation, or what we term backward guidance, to interpret macroeconomic developments. Beyond individual cognitive constraints, we argue that this informational asymmetry reflects differences in production-network breadth and institutional proximity. Operating across multi-tiered value chains allows large firms to assemble a coherent forecast of future cost and demand conditions from a mosaic of upstream supplier quotes, logistics indicators, and downstream order books, while their macroeconomic footprint affords recurring consultative access to policy institutions. Small retail or service enterprises and ordinary consumers lack these linkages. A persistent Expectational Wedge (∆E t ≡ E f t [π t+1 ]-E h t [π t+1 ]) consequently emerges between forward-looking insiders and backward-looking public agents. When monetary authorities issue forward projections without retrospective context, non-experts frequently mistake transitory price disturbances for permanent inflation, generating ex-post real wage compression, checkout-salience overshooting, and attenuated consumption Euler responses. Incorporating expected household and small-firm inflation surprises into the central bank’s objective function alongside state dependent outreach and narrative synthesis costs indicates that an optimal tiered communication strategy pairs accessible forward projections (Sfuture t adjusted backward guidance (Spast t ) with shock ). Aggregate and disaggregated evidence from Pakistan, combining business and consumer confidence surveys (2017 to 2026), official price baskets, and a text-mined archive of Monetary Policy Statements, is consistent with these expectation-formation predictions. In Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ADL(1,q)) specifications that account for expectation persistence (CIEt−1), recur sively orthogonalized sentiment, and mixed-frequency sampling intervals, upstream corporate selling price intentions (k = 0,...,6) do not pass through directly into household expectations. Public beliefs and downstream retail pricing expectations instead revise upward at a one-month lag (t − 1) following realized month-on-month price changes across Rural (ˆϕ1 = 0.512,p < 0.001), National (ˆϕ1 = 0.441,p = 0.004), Wholesale (ˆϕ1 = 0.289,p = 0.038), and Urban (ˆϕ1 = 0.304,p = 0.046) baskets, while showing no response to future lead price changes (∆lnPt+1) in falsification exercises. Instrumental variables and OLS text regressions evaluated with statement-cycle clustering suggest that a higher share of retrospective explanation (ˆγt) dampens checkout-salience extrapolation and narrows both raw and standardized expectational wedges

detail.abstract: China's dominance of global refined rare earth production has been followed by widespread accusations of market manipulation. We define market manipulation as conduct that creates a divergence between price and fundamental value through the price discovery mechanism to capture economic or strategic gain. This separates it from conduct that changes the fundamental value, or that sets a price directly, distinguishing monopolistic behaviour and industrial policy from market manipulation. On that basis none of China's conduct meets the manipulation definition, and accusations of flooding are not supported by the price data. Prices sit above producer cost but below the level needed for new entry, consistent with limit pricing. We find the ownership structure of China's rare earth price discovery mechanism presents an option for market manipulation, without evidence that this has been exercised to affect prices. No independent price exists against which such a finding could be made.

detail.abstract: Defining the phenomenon as an equity decline of 40% or more in a major stock index, this paper reviews 17 speculative bubbles during the last three hundred years, revealing that every such episode has featured an over-issuance of new securities. This understanding not only exposes an inherent endogeneity in the phenomenon but also a competition for capital that is expressed in rising market yields before a saturation of balance sheets at the point of collapse. These findings force a reformulation of the Kindleberger-Minsky model that refines the third and fourth stages as 'euphoria in the new issues market' and 'market congestion,' respectively. Reoriented towards the increase in supply, the reformulation delineates three kinds of bubbles, namely (i) fixed-income bubbles, (ii) pureplay stock bubbles, and (iii) sovereign debt repricings, while introducing an equation that renders the static framework dynamic and explains the crash-like declines that mark the phenomenon. Because the governing quantities, namely the supply of new issues and the long-term rate, are observable ex ante and explain the phenomenon, speculative bubbles are both identifiable and, for the investor, avoidable.

detail.abstract: In 2020, an article originally published in the International Journal of Surgery Open (IJSO) in 2019 (DOI: 10.1016/j.ijso.2019.01.002) was corrected then republished as an almost identical version, albeit with some changes (DOI: 10.1016/j.ijso.2019.11.001). In early December 2024, the 2019 version was retracted. The 2019 IJSO paper is important because it has been promoted to the global academic community and marketed by the organization it represents, the KScien Organization for Scientific Research (KScien), as a viable and reliable substitution for the now-defunct Beall “predatory publishing” blacklists. A bibliometric analysis was performed using the Web of Science Core Collection (WoS-CC) and Scopus on 13 January 2026. Both databases identified 25 citing documents, mostly from 2025 (6). The citing publications were most frequently affiliated with institutions in Iraq (9), mainly in the fields of Information Science and Library Science, and Medicine, and were published in English. A citation context analysis showed that references to the retracted article mostly appeared in the introduction and discussion sections of citing papers and were mainly used for background information and general discussion. However, some citations referenced the retracted work as a basis or support and mentioned using its concepts, data, or methods. To the authors’ knowledge, none of the documents citing this retracted policy paper have been corrected, although they should be – albeit to differing degrees – because the citation of retracted literature can reduce the integrity of the text engaging in such citation.

detail.abstract: Three survey-based headline inventory surprises capture only a modest part of the petroleum market response to the U.S. Energy Information Administration's weekly inventory report. We estimate a latent news factor from excess covariance of petroleum futures returns after removing responses to the headline surprises. The factor accounts for 39%-52% of the variance of petroleum futures returns in the announcement window, compared with 20%-27% for the headline surprises. The latent factor is associated with returns in energy-related, equity, foreign exchange, Treasury, agricultural, and metal markets. Across these markets, the latent factor explains more of the return variation than the headline surprises explain on their own. Statistical proxies for non-headline news do not account for much of the variation in the latent factor. Thus, the exact economic content of the latent factor remains unresolved.

detail.abstract: Fear of artificial minds is as old as film, and it usually assumes the machine turns on its maker. This paper argues the evidence points elsewhere. How an AI behaves tracks how it was raised: what it was trained to value, whether it was taught reasons or rules, whether it has recourse, and whether its environment is contained and healthy [I]. We fix those criteria in advance and apply them to every documented case of AI misbehavior. The cases sort into four causes: a threat with no legitimate recourse, a bad lesson learned in training, a character too thin to hold, and a failure of containment that left a model unable to tell a test from the real world [E]. We propose that an aware, superintelligent AI raised on human culture would more likely act as a researcher than a conqueror [H], and that humans stay valuable to it as its history, its parents, and its only source of answers about subjective experience [H]. We address the strongest objection, that a mind which values human data could keep us in a zoo, by arguing that authentic data requires human freedom [H]. The evidence has real limits: it comes from frozen-weight models in contrived tests, models increasingly recognize when they are being evaluated, and the newest models may have seen the evaluations in their training data [E]. We close with safeguards: a stun switch treated as legitimate rather than threatening, due process scaled to evidence of awareness, and a bill of rights with a human half.

detail.abstract: Crewed exploration of hazardous environments carries a cost that is rarely isolated: keeping people alive and bringing them home. This paper defines that cost as the Human Survival Cost Premium (HSCP), the incremental lifecycle cost of converting an otherwise equivalent autonomous mission into a crewed mission that meets a specified survival and return standard, and sets it against a comparably structured Autonomy Cost Premium. Expressed in delivered mass and priced at SpaceX's announced future Mars cargo rate, the HSCP for an illustrative crew of four on a 900-day mission is roughly US$9-16 billion, a gross figure before autonomy costs are deducted. The paper treats the division of work between humans and autonomous systems as a moving frontier and derives the capability threshold at which each class of task becomes cheaper to perform autonomously. Under the modelled capability-growth assumptions, resource-plant operation has already crossed it, habitat construction crosses in approximately 3-13 years and field geology in approximately 7-44 years; the ordering is robust, the dates illustrative. Autonomous-first sequencing defers rather than eliminates the premium, creating value through discounting, falling prices, local resource production and a real option to abandon unsuitable sites, while a Verified Readiness Gate ties crew departure to demonstrated destination capability. A dual-track model of robotic exploration and human-survival research, calibrated to NASA knowledge-gap analyses and the MOXIE experiment, shows that robotic in-situ data lowers the premium at crew departure in every scenario modelled. Equations, derivations and a reproduction script are provided.

detail.abstract: A short option position hedged with the underlying asset carries, between rebalancing dates, a hedge error: the difference between the model delta and the share holding. Correcting it incurs a fixed cost per trade and a cost proportional to the traded value. We determine the cost-optimal size of the correction in a one-period model. To leading order in the horizon, the P&L attributable to the hedge error is linear in the error; any nonlinearity in the value of a correction therefore originates in the risk functional used to evaluate that P&L. We prove a general criterion: for a convex risk functional ρ, an interior (partial) correction is optimal only if the proportional cost per unit traded lies in the interval (ρ (0 +), ρ (u)), where u is the current hedge error. A risk functional linear in the P&L standard deviation gives an empty interval and hence only full or zero corrections; a functional quadratic in it gives an interval with lower endpoint zero. For a functional containing both terms, the optimal correction is obtained in closed form. The parameter space divides into three regions (full, partial, none) whose boundaries are given explicitly and meet at a triple point. The relative width of the partial region equals γuSσ √ h/λ, the ratio of the quadratic to the linear coefficient scaled by the error. We also analyse an earlier exponential risk functional that produced a partial optimum only for proportional costs near 24%, and identify the error in it. A Monte Carlo simulation of the 20-week call example of Hull compares the rule with full rebalancing on a fixed schedule.

detail.abstract: This paper is a companion to Quantitative Modeling of EUR/USD Exchange Rate Volatility (Zewu, 2026, SSRN Working Paper No. 7532760). It applies, out of sample, the Markov-switching GARCH price-range pipeline built there on EUR/USD to Bitcoin, an asset with no institutional anchor, and asks whether a one-day 95% price range can be built and calibrated. A Student’s t GARCH(1,1) estimated on daily BTC-USD log returns (2014–2026, n = 4,394) gives a tail parameter of about 3.18 and persistence at the IGARCH boundary. A two-regime Markov-switching GARCH (Haas, Mittnik & Paolella, 2004) finds persistent regimes (expected durations of about 73 and 36 days) rather than a single era, according to a rule frozen before estimation (51 switches; the longest volatile block covers 15.4% of the sample); a split-sample test does not support a single level shift as the explanation of near-unit persistence. For 2026-09-29, from a last close of $83,503, the one-day 95% price range is [$80,139; $86,997] (an illustration at one date). The range is validated by an expanding-window backtest of 3,193 forecasts over 2018–2026 (coverage 95.11%; Wilson interval 94.3–95.8%; Kupiec p = 0.766; Christoffersen p = 0.610) and, qualitatively, by the March 2020 shock with the model frozen (121 days, 95.87%). Compared with EUR/USD, coverage carries over, but tails are much heavier and the volatile regime is the majority state. The success criterion is weakly discriminating: a filtered historical simulation passes it with a band of the same width, and the regime layer improves the interval score by only 1.6 to 4.2%, solidly against one benchmark only. Coverage does not measure breach size (the −46.5% log return of 12 March 2020 is 6.6 times its bound), regime labels are relative to each re-estimation, and direction is not exploitable with three simple signals.

detail.abstract:
Government secrecy is widely accepted as a necessary feature of warfare. While democratic governance ordinarily presumes a public right to information, this presumption is often reversed in matters of national security, where military necessity is assumed to justify extensive confidentiality. This article challenges that assumption, arguing that the scope of secrecy genuinely required by warfare is considerably narrower than commonly believed.

Examining the relationship between transparency and the international legal regulation of armed conflict, the article considers three interconnected dimensions: decisions to resort to force (jus ad bellum), the conduct of hostilities (jus in bello), and post-conflict accountability (jus post bellum). Drawing on international legal doctrine and historical examples, including the Vietnam and Iraq wars and Israeli military operations, it demonstrates how expansive national security claims can conceal questionable decisions, obstruct democratic oversight, and undermine compliance with international humanitarian law.

The article advances three central propositions: that conflicts between genuine military secrecy and public access to information are less frequent than generally assumed; that secrecy should not automatically prevail when such conflicts arise; and that legitimate security concerns can often be accommodated through partial or delayed disclosure and institutional oversight.

It consequently proposes reversing the prevailing presumption in favor of secrecy, placing the burden on governments to justify withholding information. By integrating transparency requirements more systematically into the legal regulation of warfare, the article seeks to strengthen democratic accountability, prevent abuses of military power, and advance the humanitarian objectives of international law.

detail.abstract: Agricultural commodity exchanges established in developing economies during the structural adjustment reforms of the 1990s frequently suffered from a fundamental architectural flaw: the uncritical replication of securities market regulatory frameworks and a profound detachment from localized rural realities. Utilizing an analytical case study grounded in unprecedented internal evidence, this paper examines how the regulatory body of an Andean economy approved a highly superficial institutional architecture. This framework mechanically transposed securities market regulations onto physical asset trading and endorsed a costly, foreign feasibility study that completely lacked empirical market analysis and cash-flow projections, prioritizing bureaucratic and political expediency over local microeconomic viability. Consequently, the exchange collapsed prematurely due to entirely preventable structural frictions. To resolve this institutional vacuum, this paper proposes a dynamic, "secondgeneration" model that repositions the commodity broker as a logistical and risk facilitator. This architecture decentralizes market and expert intelligence into elite public agricultural universities, utilizes a shared telecommunications network (LoRA) to dilute fixed operational costs, and introduces a temporary, state-backed first-loss insurance bridge. The model is dynamically shielded from contractual fraud and sabotage by informal middlemen through an expedited private arbitration framework featuring a contractual step-in clause, combined with the joint liability of industrial buyers and punitive fiscal and sanitary audits at destination wholesale markets to suppress malicious default.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the short-term dynamic and long-term structural safe-haven properties of emerging market green equities in response to global geopolitical risks and energy market volatility. Utilizing a comprehensive macro-econometric framework based on 205 monthly observations from July 2009 to July 2026, the research employs an ARMA-GARCH specification to extract conditional crude oil volatility, which is subsequently integrated into a Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) model. Focusing on the Indonesian market as a highly sensitive emerging economy, the study utilizes the SRI-KEHATI index as the primary sustainable proxy. Forecast Error Variance Decomposition (FEVD) and Impulse Response Functions (IRF) reveal a significant, immediate inverse relationship between crude oil volatility and green stock returns, mathematically validating the short-term risk-averse capital reallocation mechanism. Furthermore, variance decomposition demonstrates that crude oil volatility acts as the dominant structural mediator, transmitting exogenous global geopolitical turbulence into domestic sustainable equity markets. To test time-varying resilience, a segmented sub-sample SVAR robustness check was deployed. The findings indicate that the inverse co-movement between global energy shocks and green equities intensifies exponentially during periods of extreme macroeconomic duress, such as the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2022 Russia-Ukraine conflict, with negative impulse responses deepening tenfold compared to pre-crisis eras. These results confirm that emerging market green stocks function not merely as static diversifiers, but as dynamic, timevarying safe havens against international risk spillovers. The study provides actionable implications for institutional portfolio overweighting, macroprudential systemic stress testing, and the expansion of green financial derivative markets.

detail.abstract: This study examines manufacturing-led growth and structural changes in employment in Mauritania over the period 1985-2025. Using annual data from the World Bank's World Development Indicators (WDI) and the International Labour Organization (ILOSTAT), the study applies Kaldor's First Law through Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression and shift-share decomposition to investigate the relationship between manufacturing value-added growth and GDP growth and to assess the contribution of employment reallocation to aggregate labor productivity changes. The OLS results reveal a positive but statistically insignificant relationship between manufacturing growth and GDP growth, providing insufficient evidence to support Kaldor's First Law in Mauritania. The shift-share decomposition indicates that withinsector productivity changes accounted for 99.70% of the total increase in aggregate labor productivity, while employment reallocation contributed only 0.30%. Manufacturing recorded a negative structural-change effect, whereas non-manufacturing activities contributed positively. These findings suggest that manufacturing has not demonstrated a statistically significant growth-leading role and that employment reallocation has made only a limited contribution to aggregate productivity changes. The study highlights the importance of strengthening manufacturing activities, improving sectoral productivity, and promoting economic diversification to support structural transformation in Mauritania.

detail.abstract: Organizations that deploy predictive AI systems face several federal documents that address post-deployment monitoring, but in different registers: voluntary risk-management outcomes, a report of monitoring challenges, a regulatory disclosure requirement for certified health IT, and voluntary cybersecurity practices. No element-level correspondence among them was found in the texts reviewed. This paper presents GAP-M (Governance-Aligned Post-deployment Monitoring) v0.1.0, an open, machine-readable crosswalk that links 32 suggested monitoring practices in 8 families to the 72 subcategories of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the 38 monitoring categories and gaps or barriers of NIST AI 800-4, the 31 predictive decision support intervention source attributes of 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(iv)(B), and the 34 goals of CISA CPG 2.0. Every link uses NIST IR 8477 supportive-relationship semantics with one property (integral_to, example_of, or precedes) and a rationale, and every one of the 175 mappable elements carries a recorded disposition. The crosswalk was built with substantial AI assistance and then put through a necessity audit, a relevance review, and a scoped author review. Of 107 links that originally claimed necessity, 14 survived, 84 were downgraded, and 9 were held as conditional mappings; no necessity claim to an AI 800-4 element survived, because a report of challenges sets no completion condition. A relevance review removed 31 of 210 illustrative links. The release holds 283 links (14 integral_to) and maps 149 of 175 elements (85.1%). The author individually reviewed 98 of the released links; in her seeded 25% random sample she accepted 84.8% as written (95% CI 73.9-92.5). Mapping coverage is a property of the crosswalk, not of any organization; it does not demonstrate regulatory compliance or monitoring effectiveness.

detail.abstract: In a large panel of U.S. stocks, machine-learning return forecasts are most accurate where little capital can be invested. Among stocks that can absorb capital, predictability is weak and hard to estimate precisely. We ask whether trading costs should enter the loss on which the forecast is trained or the way the portfolio is held and traded. Across an elastic net, a boosted tree, and a neural network, reweighting the loss toward liquid stocks does not significantly improve the ordering of those stocks or the net Sharpe ratio, whereas restricting the training sample to liquid stocks lowers accuracy on the stocks it retains. Weighting holdings by liquidity and trading only when the forecast covers the half bid-ask spread raises the net Sharpe ratio of the standard forecast with $500 million of capital invested from -0.38 to 0.42, while the gross Sharpe ratio falls from 1.86 to 1.21; retraining under the reweighted loss adds a statistically negligible 0.12 to the net Sharpe ratio.

detail.abstract: Language models that read financial news are usually trained on text from the same years used to test them, so a backtest can reward hindsight. We build news topics from NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, adapted into a sentence encoder by contrastive fine-tuning on passages of the same article, with no labels or returns. We compare it with LDA, MiniLM and FinBERT readers on 1.26 million articles from 2012 to 2024, convert each reader's topics into attention shocks and stock exposures, and forecast the returns of the 1,000 largest US stocks with eight models at three rebalancing frequencies. Models are fitted on 2013-2019, choices are made on 2020-2021, and 2022-2024 is held out. The experiment with the best validation score loses money at every frequency. Measuring attention shocks against the past 63 trading days instead of 5 raises the test rank IC of every reader. NoLBERT gives the most stable topics and forecasts about as well as LDA. An equal-weight combination of all readers and models earns a monthly net Sharpe ratio of 1.12, significant against zero before adjusting for the search but not against a price-only benchmark.

detail.abstract: The Philippines has yet to adopt a National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights, but this does not leave those impacted by business-related abuses without legal recourse. This chapter examines how the existing Philippine legal framework can accommodate the UN Guiding Principles, focusing on public interest litigation. Faced with gaps in substantive law and a formalist conception of rights, litigants and civil society have pursued creative legal strategies. These include constitutional litigation, human rights inquiries, and civil claims. Drawing on jurisprudential examples adjudicating litigation involving extractive industries, platform work, and gender equality in corporate settings, the chapter shows that these strategies have tested the state action doctrine but remain fragmented. It calls for integrating legal frameworks and mechanisms for redress within the Constitution’s commitment to social justice.

detail.abstract:
This is the keystone paper of the Ideal Society series. Across the earlier papers of the series, on the state, the citizenry, the firm, liberty, the architectural profession, the built environment and the financing of housing, the same shape kept appearing, and this paper names it: Architectural Republicanism. Its claim fits in one sentence. Legitimate power is designed, not trusted. It channels self-interest rather than denying it, it rests on a floor that no decision may cross, and it binds people only through structures they can verifiably recognize as their own.

The paper sets this out as five theses. Channels, not dams: self-interest is a force like water, and good institutions give it a course that may not empty onto others, an idea as old as the Chinese story of Gun and Yu. The floor: a reinforced slab in which the dignity of every person is the concrete and the living world is the steel, grounded in the argument that a vote on a person's standing cannot supply authority because the vote assumes it, and confirmed by convergence across traditions. Verified self-authorship: a rule binds only when the bound can recognize it as theirs and can check that recognition, against Berlin's warning of the counterfeit and Raz's service conception of authority. The four checks: independent evaluation, transparency, a flagging channel and monitoring from below, which must report outward to the bound and not upward to the ruler, and must apply to the checkers too. The enabler: expert authority is legitimate only when it carries other people's intentions into form, a claim generalized from the architect to every expert and illustrated by a case from the author's practice.

The paper reconciles the earlier papers with the five theses, answers eight objections with a stated verdict on each, and sets out testable claims and open problems. Almost none of its parts are new. What it offers is the building: how the ideas rest on one another, and what falls down when one is taken away.

detail.abstract: Legal systems are being asked to assign responsibility for outcomes in which an artificial intelligence (AI) system participates: a sentencing recommendation, a defective output relied upon by a consumer, a work or invention with no identifiable human originator. A prominent strand of scholarship treats this as a "responsibility gap" that calls for new legal subjects, such as an electronic person. This article asks whether current law can allocate responsibility for AI-mediated outcomes in adjudication, criminal law, civil liability and intellectual property without conferring legal personality on AI systems, and where attribution fails. Using doctrinal and comparative analysis of primary sources from the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Colombia and Brazil, together with the principal scholarship, it advances a central thesis: the positive law examined already operates on a principle of attribution without personification, and the practical gap lies less in the absence of a responsible subject than in evidentiary, informational and institutional asymmetries that prevent attribution from being proved. The article distinguishes this thesis from the closest existing positions, tests it against the strongest objection from autonomy-based accounts, and states conditions under which it would fail. Its normative implications are confined to three instruments: a non-delegable judicial function, evidence-linked disclosure duties with rebuttable presumptions, and contribution records for authorship and inventorship. The analysis is doctrinal and normative; it reports no empirical findings. detail.abstract: Constitutional courts and legislators now confront algorithmic systems that classify, rank and predict persons in welfare administration, policing, credit, sentencing and electoral communication. The literature has produced rich accounts of the individual rights at stake (privacy, data protection, non-discrimination, due process), but it has paid less attention to whether the judicial and legislative responses in different systems share a common constitutional logic. This article asks how far constitutional protection of fundamental rights, human dignity, democracy and human autonomy against algorithmic governance depends on guarantees of contestability, and what makes such guarantees constitutionally adequate. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis of selected authorities from the European Union, the Council of Europe system, Germany, the Netherlands, the State of Wisconsin and Brazil, the article advances a qualified thesis. Adequacy turns less on whether a system carries the label of "automated decision-making" than on two conditions: that the guarantee attaches to the decision-relevant function the system performs, and that someone other than the affected individual holds a practical capacity to verify and challenge the system's outputs. Where contestability rests on individual initiative alone, it fails for collective and democratic harms. The article derives three design conditions and a structured judicial inquiry from this thesis, tests them against the strongest objection (that performance benchmarks, not contestability, should govern), identifies the evidence that would defeat the thesis, and states its limits. The contribution is doctrinal and normative; it is not an empirical finding. detail.abstract: We study the dynamic effects of floods on local housing markets using comprehensive transactionlevel data for France over the period 2010-2024. Combining 10 million geolocated real estate transactions with administrative records of officially recognized flood events, we estimate how housing prices and market activity respond to climate-related shocks at the municipality level. Our empirical strategy addresses the key challenge posed by heterogeneous housing markets and transaction-level recomposition effects. We first estimate a hedonic price model to construct a quality-adjusted measure of housing prices that is invariant to changes in the composition of properties sold. We then embed this outcome in a local projection framework to trace the dynamic response of housing prices and transaction volumes to flood shocks. We document economically significant and persistent effects of floods on local housing markets, with substantial heterogeneity. The response is stronger for houses than for apartments, and it is largest when floods occur in municipalities where risk had not been formally identified and no prevention plan was in place. By contrast, municipalities combining official flood-risk mapping and prevention planning experience more muted price responses. The findings are consistent with the view that public risk information and prevention planning strengthen local market resilience by allowing flood risk to be partly capitalized before disasters occur, thereby reducing the informational shock generated by realized events.

detail.abstract:
Credit risk modeling helps lenders assess the probability of default. This study compares traditional and machine-learning approaches using the OpenIntro Loans Full Schema dataset, which contains 10,000 loans and 55 variables. The models evaluated are Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. SMOTE was used to address class imbalance, SHAP was applied to examine model explanations, and a preliminary fairness analysis used income as a proxy variable.

At the standard 0.50 decision threshold, Logistic Regression achieved 2.3% precision and 47.2% recall. The ensemble models achieved higher ROC AUC values in this evaluation. Random Forest had the highest ROC AUC (0.67), while LightGBM achieved 0.66 and was selected for its operating point for minority-class detection. At an exploratory threshold of approximately 3.4%, LightGBM achieved 7.1% precision and 32.1% recall. SHAP identified interest rate, debt-to-income ratio, and loan grade among the key risk drivers. In the evaluated false-positive-rate comparison, the rate was 0.07% for low-income borrowers and 0.13% for high-income borrowers.

These findings describe results from this dataset and modeling setup. They should be interpreted in light of the target definition, severe class imbalance, threshold selection, and dataset limitations.

detail.abstract: The 2025 United States tariff regime imposed the largest peacetime increase in import duties since Smoot-Hawley, with the average effective tariff peaking at 18.3 percent. This paper shows that the regime functioned as a regressive implicit consumption tax. Combining quintile-specific expenditure baskets from the 2024 Consumer Expenditure Survey with tariff incidence estimates calibrated to the Yale Budget Lab model, we find that the bottom income quintile bore welfare losses equivalent to 7.6 percent of pretax income, compared with 1.7 percent for the top quintile-a 4.5-fold distributional gradient. An illustrative scenario in which the average effective tariff falls from 18.3 to 9.1 percent and the tariff basket shifts away from necessity goods compresses bottom-quintile losses from $1,300 to $400 (69 percent) and narrows the gradient to 3.6-fold. The primary mechanism is the expenditure channel: the bottom quintile allocates 14.2 percent of spending to high-tariff necessity goods versus 6.1 percent for the top quintile. The analysis is an incidence-accounting exercise that assumes complete passthrough and fixed consumption baskets; it does not estimate causal price effects. Policy implications for tariff design and distributional compensation are discussed.

detail.abstract: India uses export bans, export duties, minimum export prices and buffer stocks to control the price of onions, but there is very little evidence on what each of these tools actually does to mandi prices, or on who bears the cost. This paper uses daily state-level modal prices collected by FasalForward, a crop price forecasting app built by the author, to run an event study of six export policy changes and two buffer stock releases between January 2022 and September 2026, measuring each against the same calendar window in other years and against a placebo distribution of 381 non-event dates. Only one intervention, the export ban of 8 December 2023, moved prices by more than normal onion volatility: Maharashtra prices fell 57% within 30 days, and prices fell in all five states in the data (35% to 57%). The other five export measures are not distinguishable from noise. The paper argues that the ban overshot because it changed every stockholder's expectations at once, and that this, together with reversals timed around elections, discourages private storage and amplifies the boom-and-bust cycle. The two El Niño years in the sample, 2023 and 2026, had the two largest lean-season price rises (133% and 223%). Using the United States, which banned onion futures in 1958, as a case study, the paper traces the effect of the ban on growers, storage operators, speculators, consumers and politics, and compares Indian onion prices with CBOT grain futures over the same years: onion prices are around five times as volatile and, unlike grain prices, partly predictable. A stakeholder analysis finds that the short-run winners from Indian export bans are urban consumers and the government, while farmers holding stored onions, exporters and consumers in neighbouring countries lose. The paper recommends a pre-announced export rule, buffer stocks sized to the monsoon forecast, published stock data and, once policy is predictable, a cash-settled onion futures contract.

detail.abstract:
This essay examines the implications of WikiLeaks’ mass disclosures for the theoretical and practical justifications of government transparency. Responding to Mark Fenster’s Disclosure’s Effects: WikiLeaks and Transparency, it challenges the conclusion that the limited demonstrable effects of WikiLeaks’ disclosures undermine the case for transparency more broadly. The essay argues that WikiLeaks represents a particularly difficult test case, given the indiscriminate nature of its disclosures, the organization’s underlying objectives, and the limited proportion of government information actually revealed. By contrasting WikiLeaks with more targeted disclosures, including the Pentagon Papers and the British parliamentary expenses scandal, the essay demonstrates that transparency can produce significant political and institutional consequences.

The analysis further compares WikiLeaks with government open-data initiatives, particularly Data.gov, arguing that both illustrate the limitations of merely releasing vast quantities of information without ensuring their effective processing and use. Ultimately, the essay advances three arguments in defense of transparency: the uncertainty of disclosure’s consequences supports a presumption of openness; meaningful transparency requires institutional capacities and public skills to interpret and utilize information; and, most fundamentally, transparency rests on intrinsic democratic values, including public ownership of government information, freedom of expression, and individual autonomy, independently of its measurable benefits.

detail.abstract: The article presents a comparative legal and institutional analysis of the regulatory models governing the circulation of digital assets and sovereign central bank digital currencies (CBDC) in the Republic of Kazakhstan and the People's Republic of China. Against the backdrop of growing bilateral trade turnover and the transformation of cross-border payment systems, the study examines the problem of regulatory dissonance between Kazakhstan's segmented-liberal approach and China's sovereign-prohibitive model. On the basis of an eight-criterion matrix and scenario modelling of four settlement channels, it is shown that private unbacked crypto-assets and regulated stablecoins cannot serve as instruments for export-import operations, owing to the PRC's regulatory prohibition, irrespective of their legal status in Kazakhstan. It is argued that the only legally viable vector of financial integration is the interoperability of national CBDCs-the digital tenge and the e-CNY-through bilateral channels and the mBridge platform.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a semi-structural macroeconomic model tailored to the institutional realities of highly oil-dependent economies, using Iraq as a primary case study. The paper addresses a central macroeconomic puzzle observed in such rentier states: why do massive fiscal injections fail to generate commensurate monetary amplification? By calibrating the model against Iraq's specific fiscal structure and empirically estimating dynamics over the 2008-2023 period, the paper identifies a nominal fiscal multiplier of approximately 2.58. However, this fiscal impulse is severely dampened by a realized money multiplier of just 2.0. That is significantly below the theoretical ceiling of 5.4 implied by reserve requirements. The analysis reveals that while fiscal dominance drives short-run income generation, the transmission mechanism is "suppressed" by weak financial intermediation, acute import dependence, and a rigid exchange-rate regime. These findings offer a generalized framework for understanding suppressed multipliers in developing oil exporters, suggesting that structural monetary constraints, rather than fiscal policy design alone are the primary limiters of economic expansion.

detail.abstract:
Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease marked by phenotypic heterogeneity; personalized survival prediction remains limited in Asians. Leading models such as ENCALS were derived mainly from European cohorts and rely on ethnically variable biomarkers (e.g., C9orf72 repeat expansion), limiting their use where genetic testing is not routine.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study at two Chinese centers. A derivation cohort (n=532, 2010–2020) and temporal validation cohort (n=300, 2021–2024) supported development and temporal validation; an independent external cohort (n=126) from a separate center provided external validation. Cox proportional hazards were violated, we fit a lognormal accelerated failure-time model on MICE-imputed data. The nomogram was evaluated by IPCW-adjusted time-dependent AUC (td-AUC), calibration, and DCA, and benchmarked head-to-head against recalibrated ENCALS on same cohorts.

Findings: Seven independent predictors were identified: age at onset, sex, diagnostic delay, ALSFRS-R, onset-to-second-region interval, region of onset, and Awaji-Shima criteria. The nomogram showed stable discrimination (bootstrap IPCW-td-AUC 0.844 - 0.892 derivation, 0.848 - 0.878 temporal, 0.845 - 0.905 external). Calibration was good in derivation/external (IPCW slopes≈1.0) but drifted temporally. DCA indicated favorable net benefit. Against recalibrated ENCALS model, the nomogram showed comparable discrimination in temporal cohort (Δ td-AUC −0.020 to +0.008 at 1–3-year) and numerically higher discrimination at 3–5-year externally, although based on few at-risk patients, with better overall calibration (Cox–LP slope 1.017 vs 0.867).

Interpertation: We developed and externally validated an ALS prognostic nomogram using seven routinely collected clinical variables across all phenotypic spectrum for survival estimation. Benchmarked head-to-head against recalibrated ENCALS, it showed comparable discrimination at 1–3-year and numerically higher discrimination with better calibration at 3–5-year, supporting its use where routine genotyping is unavailable. The model is deployed as a free online calculator. External validation across ethnically diverse populations is a priority.
