detail.abstract:
Background: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) in northern Ghana is delivered door to door. Routine delivery through community-based health planning and services (CHPS) compounds is being considered, but no rule says where it would protect as many children. We developed a district-level algorithm to choose the delivery mode.

Methods: In this geospatial modelling study of 55 districts, we combined on a 1 km grid travel time to 2058 public facilities, a Bayesian spatial model of late or missed pentavalent doses (2022 Demographic and Health Survey), and district malaria cases (DHIMS2). We estimated cases averted by routine relative to campaign delivery, scaling reliability by k, how much more often a routine SMC contact slips than a vaccination contact (evidence range 1·4–2·8). These analyses formed a six-step algorithm.

Findings: 419 (17%) of 2506 routine contacts slipped, although 65% of children lived within 30 min walk of a CHPS. In 22 districts (54% of children), routine delivery would reach 90% of the campaign’s impact only if more reliable than vaccination (break-even k <1). The poorest wealth quintile (52% of children) would bear 76% of the protection lost. With clinic-linked routine delivery, the algorithm kept the campaign in all 55 districts; with outreach reaching children aged 2–4 years, it kept it in 24 (55% of children), advised measuring campaign coverage first in six (13%) and piloting in 25 (31%). Under the main calibration of k, no district met the switch threshold; 17 would if routine contacts were missed more often, but not later than vaccination contacts.

Interpretation: Routine delivery cannot replace door-to-door SMC across most of northern Ghana. The algorithm offers a transparent annual rule: keep the campaign where routine delivery would have to outperform vaccination; elsewhere, pilot with an equity safeguard and measure how late routine contacts slip before any switch.

detail.abstract:
Background: Evidence on clinical and subclinical hypothyroidism in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) is dispersed, heterogeneous, and often non-representative, limiting its use for regional burden estimation and decision making. We synthesized epidemiological, quality-of-life, economic, and equity-related evidence to assess what can and cannot be inferred from the current evidence base.

Methods: We searched 12 bibliographic databases and grey literature sources for studies published between Jan 1, 2014, and Dec 5, 2024, with no language restrictions. Eligible designs included observational studies, economic evaluations, and surveillance reports from LAC. Paired reviewers screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using NIH tools and CiCERO. We conducted random-effects meta-analyses of proportions. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251033806).

Findings: We included 145 studies from 19 LAC countries, predominantly from upper-middle-income settings. Most samples were non-probabilistic and focused on newborns or adults. Pooled prevalence was 3·6% for clinical/overt hypothyroidism (95% CI 2·7–4·6; I² 95·6%) and 9·1% for subclinical hypothyroidism (95% CI 7·2–11·4; I² 98·4%), both increasing with age. Annual incidence was 0·51% for overt hypothyroidism (95% CI 0·38–0·68) and 1·03% for subclinical hypothyroidism (95% CI 0·84–1·26). Among studies reporting sex-disaggregated data, women represented 66% of clinical/overt cases and 55% of subclinical cases. Risk-of-bias assessments rated studies included in the main meta-analyses as fair or good, but between-study heterogeneity was extreme and most samples were non-probabilistic, limiting interpretation as precise regional burden estimates. Seven studies reported health-related quality-of-life decrements, particularly in mental and social domains. Economic evidence was sparse, intervention-specific, and insufficient to quantify the regional burden.

Interpretation: Hypothyroidism is commonly reported in LAC, but extreme heterogeneity and non-probabilistic sampling preclude precise regional burden estimates. Priorities include harmonised diagnostic thresholds, population-based surveillance, sex-disaggregated reporting, and multicountry economic studies.​

detail.abstract: This is the introduction to Routledge Handbook on Artificial Intelligence and Critical Security Studies. It introduces the handbook's critical approach to the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and security, arguing that AI should not be understood simply as a technological development that creates new security challenges, but as a sociotechnical phenomenon embedded in and reshaping relations of power, knowledge, and violence. The introduction situates the study of AI within Critical Security Studies (CSS), bringing it into conversation with feminist, postcolonial and decolonial, Science and Technology Studies, and other critical approaches. It outlines four analytical registers through which the handbook approaches AI and (in)security: power, violence, knowledge, and everyday life. It also discusses the heterogeneous and contested nature of AI, highlighting the importance of examining how particular understandings and applications of AI produce specific forms of security and insecurity. Finally, the introduction presents the organization of the handbook and briefly situates its six thematic parts. In doing so, it establishes the conceptual and analytical framework through which the contributions that follow examine AI as a site of political contestation and a mechanism involved in the production of (in)security.

detail.abstract:
This work attempts to study the Secunderabad-based Chenoy Trade Centre (CTC), exemplifying a case of “embedded informality”, in the institutional structure of urban commercial space. As a matter of fact, CTC has an estimated turnover of ₹500 crore per year and comprises over 560 firms registered under the Goods and Services Tax (GST), headed by an active traders’ association. But as a case, it exhibits formal property and informal labour relations. Drawing on primary data sources (semi-structured interviews with 18 stakeholders of CTC) and theories of Hernando de Soto (2000) and Jan Breman (1996), the study concludes that informality such as this is not peripheral but an integral part of a systematic economic activity.
The findings reveal that while firms comply with formal rules with regards to their registration, taxation and transactions in the market, their labour relations are informal. Labour relations are based on oral agreements, with uncontrolled working hours (9-12 hours per day), without contracts, social security and formal labour disputes procedures. Determined based on skill differentiation, wage is unfixed and discretionary; recruitment is also done informally through friendship and acquaintance instead of institutional labour markets. There are unregulated practices in environmental aspects too, as the e-waste recyclers operate irregularly through the informal sector, which implies risks of non-compliance and health hazards.
Addressing these structural problems, the study proposes some low-cost and high-feasibility policy interventions such as: (i) targeted campaigns for e-Shram registration to separate social welfare payments from employment relations; (ii) connecting CTC to Hyderabad-based certified recyclers; (iii) gender-friendly sanitation facilities within CTC. This strategy, which leverages on established institutional actors (such as the trade association) will gradually enhance the recognition, welfare and regulation of workers, without major structural overhauls.

detail.abstract: Machine learning has the potential to reveal latent biomechanical profiles that link athlete physiology, injury predisposition, and responses to interventions to reducing injury risk. This study developed a manifold-learning-based clustering approach to stratify athletes into biomechanically distinct subgroups. We evaluated combinations of four dimensionality-reduction techniques (t-SNE, KPCA, Diffusion Maps, Autoencoders) with three clustering algorithms (GMM, Agglomerative, DBSCAN) on biomechanical data from 312 female athletes (soccer, volleyball, or basketball) during a drop vertical jump (DVJ), selecting the optimal pipeline. All participants received a neuromuscular training (NMT) intervention aimed at reducing anterior cruciate ligament injury risk and were additionally randomized to receive either augmented NMT (aNMT) or sham NMT (sNMT), respectively involving accurate or uninformative visual feedback about training exercise performance. The optimal pipeline (t-SNE with GMM) identified three biomechanically distinct clusters that aligned with sport type, injury incidence, and intervention allocation. Profiles included a moderate-risk group, an injury-resilient group, and a high-risk, injury-prone group with elevated sprains, concussions, and non-preventable injuries, demonstrating that athletes can be grouped based on latent biomechanical structure using this approach. Cluster validity was confirmed by silhouette scores (0.49) and statistical testing at 95% confidence for separation of sport (0.00002), injury (0.036), and intervention (0.017). These results demonstrate that learned manifolds capture physiologically meaningful structure, offering a generalizable framework for stratifying athletes into biomechanically distinct subgroups associated with injury patterns, sport participation, and the distribution of interventions.

detail.abstract: This paper studies a behavioral model of persuasion where the receiver may misinterpret information designed by the sender. Instead of assuming perfect observation, we allow the receiver to mistake one message for another with some probability. This misinterpretation limits the sender's ability to influence beliefs and disrupts the standard concavification method of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011). We also study a second departure in non-Bayesian updating: naïveté, where the receiver fails to account for misinterpretation. Misinterpretation weakly harms the sender without affecting the receiver, but naïveté can benefit the sender at the receiver's expense. In a binary example, we illustrate how misinterpretation reduces the sender's optimal payoffs, and when naïveté lowers the receiver's demand for information. We then extend the analysis to confirmation bias, where misinterpretation depends endogenously on beliefs and strategy. Our analysis complements prior work on non-Bayesian inference (de Clippel and Zhang, 2022) and symmetric noise (Tsakas and Tsakas, 2021), by focusing on structured misunderstanding in persuasion.

detail.abstract: Modern growth theory has largely accepted the purely labor-augmenting representation of technical change that Uzawa's theorem appears to require. We show that the aggregate accounts cannot reveal the direction of technical change. The accounts identify the effective factor supplies-the engines of growth-and stop at their boundary: how each engine's growth divides between accumulation of the factor and its augmentation is a property of the technology, and output, payments and shares, all unchanged when either factor's unit is rescaled, do not reveal it. The classification as Harrod-, Hicks-or Solow-neutral is therefore supplied by a designation-the rules by which capital and labor are counted-standing in for the omitted data. This relocates the question of the direction of technical change from mechanism to observation. Classifications under different designations differ by exactly the growth of the conversion between their units, so the received convention can be tested rather than merely questioned. For the United States over 1985-2019, the accounts' designation reads the path as nearly purely labor-augmenting; two independently constructed alternatives, counting capital as employer firms or as machines on Greenwood, Hercowitz and Krusell's calibration, converge on a near-Hicks-neutral reading of the same path.

detail.abstract: How does a receiver integrate what a sender says with why she says it? When a sender interprets data to influence a receiver's beliefs about an uncertain state, the receiver faces two perspectives simultaneously: the strategic perspective, what the sender's choice of interpretation reveals about her private information, and the semantic perspective, what her interpretation literally implies about the state. This paper develops a framework that accommodates both and characterizes a class of inferential behaviors. We axiomatize the receiver's inferential rule and show it admits a representation as a convex combination of strategic and semantic content, parameterized by a single weighting parameter λ. The framework unifies cheap talk (λ = 0) and model persuasion (λ = 1) as special cases of a common primitive, and yields tractable comparative statics on how the inferential rule shapes equilibrium. For intermediate λ, the sender's semantic choice and the receiver's reliance on the semantic perspective generate novel tradeoffs: semantic content anchors beliefs, feasibility of communication expands, and even negligible reliance on semantic content makes the cheap talk benchmark a knife-edge, not a robust prediction.

detail.abstract: The article solves the scholarly task of constructing a single standard for the legal qualification of any use of force against a maritime vessel, in particular attack, detention, arrest, confiscation and transfer of the vessel to another owner, irrespective of which State or non-State actor acts and in which maritime space. The study continues the author's work on an attack on a merchant vessel as a war crime and an act of aggression and extends the test formulated therein to the events of 2014-2026 in the Black, Azov, Baltic, Red and Mediterranean Seas, the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, the Strait of Hormuz, the Caribbean, and the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. A triage of three mutually exclusive legal regimes is proposed: the conduct of hostilities, law enforcement under the law of the sea, and the extraterritorial use of lethal force outside armed conflict. The choice of regime is determined by the threshold of armed conflict under the Tadić test, the objective status of the vessel at the moment force is used, and the nature of the act. On the basis of more than one hundred individually identified vessels, it is shown that, as of October 2026, none of the detentions of vessels of the so-called shadow fleet in Europe has ended in final confiscation: vessels were released, including after payment of a fine, or remain under arrest, and only in isolated cases was there a transfer of the vessel to another State or a removal of cargo. It is established that the seizures of tankers off Venezuela by the United States were accompanied by the sale of oil through private traders and by the holding of the proceeds in an account in a third State, which raises well-founded questions of transparency, although no private interest has been established by a court. The judicial fate of the tankers Tifani (IMO 9273337) and Majestic X, also known as Phonix (IMO 9198317), seized by the United States in the Indian Ocean in April 2026, is traced: a federal court refused the Government a secret sale of the seized property, and more than six hundred victims of terrorism holding court judgments against Iran for almost four billion dollars have claimed rights to the cargo of Iranian oil valued at 130–140 million dollars, which exposes the competition between prize law, confiscation under terrorism legislation and the enforcement of court judgments against the property of a State. The application to the detention of crews of the standard set by the judgment of the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights in Medvedyev and Others v. France of 29 March 2010 is substantiated. Ukrainian practice of arrest, confiscation and nationalisation of vessels since 2018 and its relationship with Article 2 of Hague Convention VI of 1907 are examined. The widespread belief that the IMO number changes when a vessel is converted into a warship is refuted: the number is permanent throughout the entire service life of the vessel, while conversion removes the vessel from the scope of the SOLAS Convention and subjects it to Articles 1–6 of Hague Convention VII of 1907. Intelligence-gathering vessels and the legal consequences of their detention are analysed, in particular the judgment of the Helsinki Court of Appeal of 27 August 2026 in the Eagle S case. Strikes on merchant vessels in the exclusive economic zones of Romania, Bulgaria and Türkiye and in ports of the Russian Federation are examined in the light of Articles 1 and 2 of Hague Convention XIII of 1907, and it is shown that the rise of war-risk insurance premiums in the Black Sea to two per cent of the vessel’s value and the extension of the listed area to the entire Black Sea in September 2026 reversed the downward trend in freight rates observed in 2024–2025. The scholarly novelty lies in combining the three regimes in a single operational algorithm and in testing it against the full body of events, with the refinement of factual data of earlier publications, as well as in identifying a gap in the national mechanism for compensating damage caused to vessels and seafarers.

detail.abstract: Occupational heat exposure may increase injury risk through thermal strain, fatigue, dehydration, reduced vigilance, and changes in work organisation. Evidence from several countries supports an association between extreme heat and workplace injuries, but the size and shape of this association cannot be assumed to be identical across Sub-Saharan Africa. This study develops and audits a country-year framework for investigating temperature extremes and occupational injury mortality in the region. The evidence package includes a 49-country candidate panel for 1990-2024, population data, eight ILOSTAT labour-market indicators, and a Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 export. The workbook contains 1,715 candidate country-year records. The supplied labour-market indicators have uneven coverage: modelled labour-force participation has 1,607 non-missing values, modelled unemployment and employment-to-population ratios each have 1,561, while observed informal employment has 171. The GBD export supplies endpoint-change estimates for broad injury burden across selected locations; it does not provide annual occupational injury deaths attributable to environmental heat. The present analysis therefore distinguishes the observed data audit from the planned inferential study. It proposes consistent occupational injury definitions, gridded heat metrics, fixed-effects panel models, uncertainty reporting, and sensitivity analyses for missingness, thresholds, and spatial aggregation. The framework provides a reproducible route to estimating associations once annual occupational injury outcomes and climate data are harmonised, while avoiding unsupported attribution of general injury deaths to workplace heat.

detail.abstract: Higher energy costs place a disproportionately heavy burden on low-income households. While prior research tends to examine energy-related financial literacy, cognitive constraints, engagement, and energy poverty largely in isolation, we provide a two-group structural equation modeling approach that jointly models these factors in a single framework. Using an online survey (n = 1,281) with an oversampling of low-income households and a focus on electricity tariff switching behavior, we identify how psychological and structural factors shape consumer energy behavior. Cognitive barriers directly undermine the acquisition of tariff knowledge. Across both income groups, electricity tariff literacy robustly predicted switching considerations, while engagement emerged as a stronger driver of behavioral change than knowledge alone. detail.abstract: We compare the manufacturing capabilities of the United States and China with a focus on the most advanced goods and critical industries. We find that the two nations have followed different trajectories in the 21st century; China’s capabilities (in terms of revealed comparative advantage) have now surpassed those of the United States. We offer a suite of policy reforms to repair noted weaknesses in the U.S. industrial commons; no single, “silver-bullet” governmental action will reverse the generational decline in domestic production capabilities.

detail.abstract: This chapter analyses open source as a techno-regulatory strategy for advancing digital sovereignty, defined as "the capacity to understand, develop, and regulate digital technologies and thereby exercise self-determination and control over digital assets". We argue that open source is increasingly leveraged as a strategy to undermine competitors, shifting where value is captured. Hence, open source should not be understood as in opposition to Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) but as an ecosystem built upon them: open licenses require a functioning IPRs to be enforceable, and they reconfigure rather than abolish exclusive rights, opening alternative possibilities for transparency, collaboration, and redistribution. Crucially, we contend that open source is typically mobilized as a complement to proprietary strategies, not a substitute for them. Even where code or artificial intelligence model weights are open, actors continue to build power by owning knowledge assets, including trade secrets, tacit knowledge, proprietary datasets, and compute, so that openness frequently relocates value capture to adjacent layers of the stack rather than dissolving it. We argue that the capacity of openness to strengthen sovereignty depends less on the license than on the governance, industrial, and capability conditions surrounding it. After having discussed how large technology corporations have successfully leveraged open source, we offer three cases to illustrate how our findings apply to state policy through a graduated logic. Brazil shows how open licenses secure legally irrevocable access as a defensive shield, yet access without domestic capability merely relocates dependency. South Korea shows how embedding open source within developmental-state industrial policy converts access into codevelopment capability and export strength. India shows how open, modular Digital Public Infrastructure can be turned into standard-setting power, exporting not only software but a model of digital governance. In conclusion, we emphasize that for emerging economies-and all those who may be considered as "developing countries" in digital terms, i.e. most countries-, open source becomes sovereignty-enhancing only within a long-term, patient and focused ecosystemic strategy combining openness with sustained investment in institutions, skills, and industrial capabilities.

detail.abstract: Firms' shipping technology choices shape delivery lags and the production consequences of supply chain disruptions. detail.abstract: We develop a cognitive asset valuation framework grounded in associative memory and perceptual salience. In our model, contemporaneous return shocks act as cues that selectively recall similar past experiences to anchor an endogenous memory norm, while bounded attention adjusts toward perceptual surprises relative to this benchmark. Historical return dispersion serves as a cognitive filter. The resulting metric, Decision Value (DV), distorts prices and negatively predicts cross-sectional equity returns. In the US equity market, a long-short portfolio sorted on DV generates a monthly return spread of1.857% (t=13.36), yielding multi-factor alphas in excess of 1.729% that remain robust to standard characteristic controls, including short-term reversal, salience, and prospect theory. Decomposing DV confirms that neither the memory norm nor salience alone drives the result; predictability requires their synthesis. The return premium is concentrated during intraday trading, amplified by unrealized capital losses, and strongest among retail-dominated, arbitrage-constrained securities. Internationally, the effect persists across developed markets but attenuates in emerging markets due to structural non-stationarity.

detail.abstract: Integrated source–grid–load–storage (SGLS) systems involve complex interest coordination among multiple stakeholders, and heterogeneity in their perceptions of payoff information may affect strategic choices and collaborative evolution. This study incorporates perceptual heterogeneity into an evolutionary game framework and develops a four-player evolutionary game model involving source–storage entities, grid companies, the government, and electricity trading platforms. The evolutionary stable strategies and critical conditions of each stakeholder are analyzed, and the mechanisms through which the cost–benefit structure determines the direction of strategy evolution and perceptual heterogeneity shapes the evolutionary process are elucidated. The results show that the four stakeholders exhibit pronounced strategic differentiation under a given cost–benefit structure. Perceptual heterogeneity does not alter the sign of payoff differences, the theoretical critical conditions, or the direction of the long-run equilibrium; rather, it reshapes the evolutionary process by changing stakeholders’ responsiveness to payoff differences, resulting in significant acceleration or delay effects. Specifically, when the payoff difference is positive, optimistic perceptions facilitate the diffusion of proactive strategies; conversely, when the payoff difference is negative, they accelerate the withdrawal from proactive strategies. These findings provide a theoretical basis for optimizing benefit-coordination and incentive mechanisms in integrated SGLS systems and promoting stable long-term collaboration among multiple stakeholders.

detail.abstract: Sustainable energy systems require major electricity grid expansion, yet the environmental impacts of future grid infrastructure are largely overlooked. We assess these impacts by combining a detailed model of Germany’s grid infrastructure with Integrated Assessment Model scenarios reflecting future supply chains. While more renewables help decarbonize grid component production, transmitting and distributing this renewable electricity requires additional grid expansion, raising emissions. We find that grid infrastructure becomes a major contributor to climate impacts of future electricity, with shares rising from 1% in 2023 to up to 21% by 2045. Main drivers of grid-related impacts, even under ambitious decarbonization, remain electricity and heat generation for aluminum production alongside emissions from steelmaking. Moreover, decarbonizing supply chains shift environmental impacts towards land use and mineral depletion. Our findings underscore the growing environmental relevance of grid infrastructure, reveal levers for reducing grid-related impacts, and call for their integration into global policy and energy planning.

detail.abstract: Pastoral appointments in The Apostolic Church Nigeria are recently believed to depend more on personal connections, popularly called "man-knows-man," than merit. Unlike those days of the first indigenous National President late Pastor E. E. Okon where pastoral calling was said to be based on spiritual appointment and by merits, these days, these factors have been neglected and strange factors such as man-knows-man have taken over. This study therefore examined the influence of nepotism, patronage, and neglect of merit criteria (spiritual level, educational level, and ministerial exposure) on church growth in The Apostolic Church Nigeria. A descriptive survey of the correlational type was adopted with a sample of 400 respondents (100 pastors and 300 members) drawn from two fields in Cross River State through proportionate stratified random sampling and completed the researcher-developed Nepotism, Patronage and Church Growth Questionnaire (overall Cronbach's alpha = .93). Four null hypotheses were tested at the .05 level using Pearson correlation and multiple regression. Nepotism (r =-.46), patronage (r =-.44), and neglect of merit criteria (r =-.61) were each significantly and negatively related to church growth (all p < .001). Jointly, the three predictors explained 40.7% of the variance in church growth, F(3, 396) = 90.72, p < .001; neglect of merit criteria (β =-.47) and nepotism (β =-.19) were significant unique predictors, while patronage was not (β =-.09, p = .083). It was concluded that appointment on relational rather than merit grounds is associated with weaker church growth. The church is therefore encouraged to adopt transparent, criteria-based appointment procedures, widen participation in appointment decisions, and invest in pastoral training and exposure.

Using individual-level Survey of Professional Forecasters data, we classify forecasters by their relative positions in federal spending and real GDP forecast distributions. We find pronounced initial asymmetry: lower-tail fore casters exhibit substantially weaker pass-through than upper-tail forecasters, reflect ing more pessimistic responses to fiscal news. detail.abstract: Pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, foundations, and family offices routinely claim patience and a long-term horizon as structural advantages. But while public equity is a meaningful allocation for all of them, it is unclear how much exposure is actually built to leverage patience and time horizon. Resolving this conundrum is the central aim of this paper. To clarify, we call an active public-equity exposure ‘long-horizon’ only when four things are true at once: the portfolio is meaningfully different from its benchmark; its return comes from the economic performance of the underlying businesses rather than from the repricing of their shares; the capital underpinning it can stay invested through stretches of relative underperformance; and it is judged based on how those businesses perform and on whether the manager held to the process they described, with relative return never decisive inside five years. On this standard, we hypothesize that most long-term investors are ‘underweight long term’ in active public equity. The cause of the public-equity short-termism of these investors, we argue, is a cascade: evaluation pressure runs from boards to chief investment officers, and from CIOs to managers. The mandates that result from this cascade depend on the market re-rating a holding within roughly three to twenty-four months. We call that time-band the middle horizon. Each link in the cascade behaves rationally given the incentives it faces. But the chain as a whole screens for mandates that show near-term validation, and managers adapt their research, portfolio construction, risk systems, communications, and hiring to the clocks that govern the capital they are given. Stated as four conditions, long-termism becomes something an investor can measure across its own book. And the claim to be a long-term investor emerges as a claim that can actually be checked.

detail.abstract: Market risk backtests are usually designed by analysts who have already seen the test data, so a reader cannot distinguish a specification fixed in advance from one chosen because it passed. We report a pre-registered backtest. For a portfolio of US Treasury, inflation breakeven and euro positions, every hypothesis, test, decision rule and power calculation was fixed on 1988–2014 data, and a fingerprint of the registered files was anchored in the Bitcoin blockchain. The anchor proves what was registered; the order of registration and evaluation rests on the author's logs. On the 2015–25 record (2,736 trading days), a Gaussian value-at-risk model with a frozen covariance matrix passed unconditional coverage tests at 97.5% and 99%, but, as predicted, its exceptions clustered: the Basel traffic light turned yellow in 2020 and 2022 and red in 2023. An unregistered check with every position reversed finds no significant clustering at 97.5% and no red light. At 97.5%, an exponentially weighted variance removed the clustering and scored significantly better under a rule fixed in advance. A covariance calibrated on 2007–9 took about a quarter of the expected exceptions yet never left the green zone. A conditional expected shortfall test rejected every specification. We set out the registration as a checklist that model validators can reuse.

detail.abstract: Karachi, Pakistan's largest metropolitan city and economic powerhouse, faces an acute urban housing crisis exacerbated by rapid population growth, internal migration, and a lack of affordable, safe accommodation options for solo dwellers such as students, professionals, and short-term migrants. This research investigates the feasibility and potential of introducing coliving or co-housing communities in Karachi as a sustainable solution for solo dwellers. detail.abstract:
India's existing framework for trade secret protection relies on a fragmented combination of contract law, the equitable doctrine of breach of confidence, the Information Technology Act, 2000, and relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. This framework raises questions about the adequacy and enforceability of protection against contemporary forms of cyber-economic espionage, including digital data exfiltration, insider threats, and cross-border misappropriation of confidential commercial information.

This paper critically evaluates the Indian legal framework through doctrinal analysis, comparative legal research, and a normative law-and-economics approach. It examines the trade secret protection regimes of the United States, the European Union, China, and Singapore to identify legislative and institutional approaches that may be adapted to the Indian context. It also evaluates the Law Commission of India's Report No. 289 and the proposed Protection of Trade Secrets Bill, 2024, assessing their capacity to address the legal and procedural challenges associated with digital misappropriation.

The paper identifies structural limitations concerning the definition and legal character of trade secrets, the reach of contractual remedies, the evidentiary challenges of cyber-enabled theft, and the availability of specialised civil and criminal remedies. In response, it proposes a hybrid legislative framework titled the Trade Secrets (Protection, Enforcement and Economic Security) Act. The proposed model incorporates a digital-era definition of trade secrets, enhanced civil remedies, safeguards for employee mobility and legitimate disclosure, and a differentiated approach to ordinary misappropriation and economic espionage. It further considers institutional enforcement and India-specific concerns involving regulatory data, traditional knowledge, data protection, and national economic security.

The paper argues that a dedicated statutory framework could improve legal certainty and enforcement while balancing commercial confidentiality with competition, employee mobility, public interest, and the legitimate circulation of knowledge. It concludes by proposing a context-sensitive legislative approach informed by comparative experience and India's constitutional and international obligations.

detail.abstract: A common implementation of the deflated Sharpe ratio estimates the maximum of the null distribution by freezing the candidate set a search produced, and resampling it. When a search is adaptive, the frozen set is not equal to the process, and the resampling produces a given error. The direction, size, and remedy for the error have been determined. detail.abstract: We introduce a novel measure of how European Central Bank (ECB) monetary policy is interpreted by analysts at major investment banks. We construct a “policy interpretation shock” based on the language used in analysts’ reports covering monetary policy decisions by the ECB’s Governing Council (GovC). The main identifying assumption is that changes in the way analysts report on policy communication by the GovC—that is, the change in the policy tone from the preview report to the recap report—reflect unexpected information revealed by the policy event. Using GPT-based sentiment extraction, we show that the tone in these reports closely tracks that of the GovC, often even anticipating shifts in tone. Changes in the policy tone before and after meetings capture how market intermediaries interpret and adjust their assessment of policy decisions. These interpretation shocks are followed by contractionary macroeconomic responses and systematic movements in financial-market prices. These findings underscore the important role of communication in shaping expectations and influencing economic outcomes.

detail.abstract: The author proposes an understanding of decolonial constitutionalism that accounts for the history of slavery, colonialism, and racial capitalism not only as historical injustices but also as constitutive forces of power, knowledge, and being. The 1661 Barbados Slave Code as a “slave constitution” institutionalized racialized violence in the slave society to render the Black human as nonhuman through the law. The author critiques the coloniality of Independence Caribbean constitutions and challenges the reformist approaches to decolonial constitutionalism that fail to disrupt this coloniality. Employing Charles W. Mills's use of the creole concept of smadditizin’—the struggle for recognition of personhood where it was denied because of race—the author advocates for a refounding of Caribbean constitutions. This refounding must center the Caribbean person as “somebody” (smaddy), as individual and collective agents of their own liberation. The author therefore envisages decolonial constitutionalism as a transformative project to create a new blueprint for the way of life of a political community, that is, a constitution that affirms the sovereignty of the people. Decolonial constitutionalism is not merely legal reform; it must be an ontological rupture grounded in Caribbean-centered epistemologies.

detail.abstract: How does heterogeneity in banks’ interest-rate risk exposure shape monetary policy transmission? We develop a quantitative macroeconomic model of heterogeneous banks to answer this question. We establish an irrelevance result: differences in interest-rate risk exposure between fixed- and variable-rate banking systems matter for transmission only when bank solvency concerns become relevant. Calibrating the model to the euro area, we show that idiosyncratic default risk pushes a substantial share of banks toward the solvency threshold, making heterogeneity quantitatively important. When policy rates rise, fixed-rate banks suffer net interest margin compression—funding costs increase while legacy loan income stays unchanged—eroding capital and triggering sharper deleveraging. The lending elasticity to monetary policy is one-third larger in fixed-rate economies. The effects extend to financial stability: tightening raises bank failure rates in fixed-rate systems while lowering them in variable-rate systems. The results provide a rationale for macroprudential and monetary policy coordination and for monetary policy gradualism.

detail.abstract: Why do stock markets appear resilient to geopolitical risk? Using firm-level measures of geopolitical risk exposure and data on investment funds’ holdings, we show how funds help swiftly restore valuations compressed during bouts of heightened geopolitical risk. More intense geopolitical shocks strengthen this stabilizing role. Declines in valuations of exposed but otherwise sound firms raise expected returns, attracting funds to acquire these assets at depressed prices, consistent with a search for yield mechanism. This behavior is more pronounced among funds with greater risk-taking capacity and weaker past performance. Funds’ tilt toward exposed stocks increases portfolio concentration, partly offset by higher cash buffers. In contrast, ultimate investors withdraw from exposed funds. The results are not driven by any particular industry—including defense or dual-use production—and are robust to a rich set of controls, fixed effects, and placebo tests.

detail.abstract: We study institutional cash management by constructing a novel dataset that records the specific money market funds (MMFs) held by each mutual fund in each month from 2010 to 2024. We document remarkably high inertia: more than half of mutual funds never switched their MMF choice throughout the sample period, despite non-negligible yield dispersion. To decompose the sources of this inertia, we develop a two-stage structural model that separately identifies the determinants of portfolio managers' attentiveness ("waking up") and their conditional preferences once attentive. We estimate the model using a methodology that combines BLP-style contraction mapping with maximum likelihood. We establish three main findings. First, MMFs with less attentive investor bases engage in greater liquidity transformation while offering lower yields. As a result, they earn higher profits and exhibit significantly higher survival rates, especially during periods of low interest rates. Second, we find that aggregate flows appear more yield-sensitive during low interest rate periods (the well-documented "reaching for yield" phenomenon) not because individual investors become more yield-seeking, but because a larger fraction of investors becomes attentive - a composition effect rather than a preference shift. Third, counterfactual analysis reveals a potential tension between market efficiency and financial stability if AI-driven automation reduces investor inattention. In the absence of inattention, fees fall by approximately half, yield dispersion collapses to near zero, and market concentration declines by roughly 20%, but monthly fund flows increase by about three times and the incidence of fund-months in which redemptions exceed a fund's weekly liquid assets rises by about six times, raising the risk of fire sales and MMF runs.

detail.abstract: Automated markets increasingly host autonomous, learning trading agents and are powered by formulaic automated market makers (AMMs). Three behavioral archetypes are modeled as agentic reinforcement learning (RL) systems: a rational arbitrageur, a manipulator, and a retail herd-follower. Each archetype is defined by its reward function within a common, asset-agnostic exposure-control environment, and each is trained with a value-based Deep Q-Network (DQN) and with REINFORCE using a learned baseline. A pilot on hourly cryptocurrency data (AAVE, ETC, SUI) motivates the hypotheses. title: Frozen Exemplar Response Learning: self-measured teaching states for local learning and reconfigurable memory in physical neural networks

detail.title: Frozen Exemplar Response Learning: self-measured teaching states for local learning and reconfigurable memory in physical neural networks
detail.abstract: Physical neural networks compute with real signals. Their training usually requires an error signal computed outside the system or transported back through it. Local learning avoids this transport but still needs a target state at every layer. In most local schemes, this target is a code derived from the class label and written into the layer from outside. In Frozen Exemplar Response Learning (FERL), the target is a state that the layer itself produced in response to a real exemplar, recorded before learning and held fixed. No external number enters the network. The target and the current state are signals of the same layer in the same units, so they can be compared where they occur. A simple local update reduces their difference. No error is transported between layers. A test sample is assigned to the class of the nearest stored output state. Residual identity paths carry this learning to deep networks without loss of accuracy. Because the stored states are states of the network itself, new ones can be recorded while the weights stay fixed. States recorded at further rotations of handwritten digits extend the range of angles estimated by the trained network. An untrained network with the same recorded states estimates the angle equally well. Synaptic learning adds a second property: observations lie closer to the recorded states, so their distance from these states flags an input outside the recorded range. The same distance ranks decisions by reliability: withholding the least separated tenth of the test samples raises the accuracy on the rest by more than four percentage points on Digits and on MNIST. Learning is thus divided between slow synaptic weights that shape the representation and fast reference states that can be extended without any weight update. For physical hardware several consequences follow. The teaching states are measured on the hardware itself, so training needs no model of its nonlinearities. The stored states need two bits per value, whereas the synaptic weights need fine resolution. Strongly sparse connections suffice. Adaptation after training is an operation of the reference memory, with the weights fixed.

title: ECG-FDConv: A frequency-dynamic convolutional architecture for atrial fibrillation recognition

detail.title: ECG-FDConv: A frequency-dynamic convolutional architecture for atrial fibrillation recognition
detail.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) remains a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity and imposes a substantial global health burden, yet its paroxysmal and asymptomatic nature renders timely diagnosis difficult with electrocardiography (ECG). Existing deep learning strategies for AF detection are constrained by fixed receptive fields and static kernel weights, which limit their capacity to capture both transient beat-level morphological details and longer-range rhythmic regularities. To this end, we construct ECG-FDConv, a frequency-dynamic convolutional framework that jointly optimises spectral diversity and temporal adaptability without increasing parameter cost. This model consists of three modules: Fourier Disjoint Weight (FDW) constructs the frequency-diverse kernels from a fixed parameter budget by partitioning Fourier domain according to physiologically meaningful bands; Kernel Temporal Modulation (KTM) utilizes element-wise, input-dependent scaling to enable fine-grained morphological adaptation, and Frequency Band Modulation (FBM) introduces temporally variant modulation across distinct clinical frequency sub-bands. Extensive experiments across two public databases demonstrate that ECG-FDConv consistently outperforms several representative convolutional baselines with an accuracy of 99.0%. Theoretical convergence analysis confirms stable and rapid optimisation dynamics and visualizations are further provided to interpret clinical decisions. ECG-FDConv offers a robust and parameter-efficient and interpretable solution for automated AF classification with potential for deployment in hospital and primary-care settings to facilitate earlier therapeutic intervention.

detail.abstract: Using a novel detection mechanism, I study non-compliance with disclosure requirements for operating lease commitments (OLCs) under IAS 17 in Italy. I first analyze the determinants of firms' non-compliance and then assess whether the revelation of their previously undisclosed OLCs has consequences for their cost of equity. In the determinants analysis, I predict and find that such non-compliance is positively and significantly associated with pre-existing financial leverage. I also find some evidence of an association with having a Big 4 auditor. detail.abstract: In this paper, we consider the role expectations play in the spatial diffusion of monetary shocks through a network economy. Using an overlapping generations network model, it is shown that changing the assumption of expectations from rational to adaptive, flips the economic response of a monetary expansion. We consider the Pareto efficiency of this economy, and how expectations change the welfare effects of monetary policy. Different network structures are explored, and we discuss how monetary conditions and convergence to steady-state relate to these network structures. The heterogeneous agent case is considered, and the response is shown to depend crucially on the spatial organization of agents and who initially receives the monetary expansion, leading to varying short and medium-run effects.

detail.abstract: We study dynamic supply-demand matching in markets where heterogeneous participants arrive over time, generate pair-specific rewards, and may leave before being matched. The platform must balance the prospect of a more valuable match against the risk of losing an available participant. We propose a Split-and-Match algorithmic framework guided by a linear programming benchmark that distinguishes the two arrival orders of each matched pair. The framework uses directional matching flows to allocate matching opportunities and generate candidates online. We develop and analyze implementations under high-volume arrivals and general arrivals, with the general-arrival analysis also covering general graphs. We then adapt the general-arrival implementation to demand-side rejection, accounting for the fact that a refusal removes the demand but leaves the supply available. We establish constant-factor performance guarantees for these implementations. We also establish upper bounds on the worst-case ratios achievable by any online algorithm relative to the offline optimum and the linear programming benchmark. Numerical experiments calibrated using New York City taxi data show that the proposed algorithms earn higher rewards than the benchmark policies across the tested settings, including those with rejection, while revealing a trade-off between matching rewards and waiting times.

detail.abstract: Heterogeneous risk affects not only who joins a peer-to-peer insurance pool but also how intensively participants share losses. We study a P2P pool in which individuals choose continuous contribution rates, and compare a planner's type-contingent allocation subject to participation and incentive-compatibility constraints with a decentralized benchmark in which each participant independently chooses her own rate. Under independent risks, type-neutral welfare weights, positive low-risk variance, and at least two participants of each type, the planner's problem reduces to a one-dimensional search over boundary allocations, and full pooling is optimal if and only if the mean-loss gap between types is at or below an explicit threshold. We prove that every global planner optimum has a strictly higher low-risk contribution rate and strictly higher welfare than every active Nash equilibrium with a positive low-risk contribution rate. Low-risk participants do not internalize the diversification benefit they provide to high-risk participants. At the benchmark low-risk entry cutoff, a small reduction in the high-risk contribution rate allows the planner to retain a substantial positive low-risk contribution rate, whereas the market excludes low-risk participants. In the benchmark calibration, this composition wedge generates a welfare loss of about 22% of the planner's attainable surplus over autarky.

detail.abstract: How strongly do markets expect the Federal Reserve to respond to economic news? We measure this market-perceived policy rule in real time using prediction markets. Kalshi prices both the coming CPI print and the next FOMC decision, so inflation news can be measured against the market's own expectation minutes before the release, and the policy response read from prices within the same hour. Combined with fed funds futures and Kalshi contracts on later CPI prints, this simultaneous measurement links the expectation of today's print, the policy response and expectations of future prints, rather than pairing a price response with a survey consensus collected days earlier. Over 2021-2026, a 1 percentage point upside CPI surprise raises the expected rate at the next FOMC meeting by 18 basis points, and other major releases move it with the signs a policy rule implies. Measured against the survey consensus instead, the same price changes imply a response a fifth to a quarter weaker. The response builds along the policy path, from 13 basis points at one month to about 72 at eleven months, and the same news raises the expected next CPI print. A hot print thus raises expected policy far beyond the next meeting and expected near-term inflation, all within the hour.

detail.abstract: Amidst growing concerns of declining work participation of women in India, an area of further apprehension has been the rapidly dropping work participation of women from the tribal communities. Primary data has been collected from 400 Reang women residing in twenty villages distributed over South Tripura and Gomati districts. Nearly thirty per cent of the surveyed Reang women in their prime ages were found to be non-working. Other significant variables affecting the decision to work are husband's education level, household standard of living, family size, household structure and women's mobility. It points towards the distinct possibility of socioeconomic segmentation of women's occupational choices and that Reang women with higher education may not be working for lack of suitable job opportunities.

detail.abstract: The growing popularity of artificial intelligence (AI) has created opportunities for innovation while also enabling fraudulent practices in the technology and venture capital industries. This article discusses AI washing, the practice of falsely advertising or exaggerating a product’s AI capabilities to attract investors, customers, and funding. Through examples involving Nate Inc., Presto Automation, and enforcement actions by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Federal Trade Commission (FTC), the article illustrates how companies have misrepresented automation by relying on human workers to perform tasks marketed as AI-driven. It also explores the factors that enable these schemes, including investor fear of missing out, insufficient technical due diligence, and limited understanding of AI infrastructure. Beyond financial losses, AI washing undermines public trust, disadvantages legitimate AI developers, and diverts capital from genuine technological innovation. It is concluded by emphasizing the importance of transparent performance metrics, technical verification, and regulatory accountability. By encouraging investors, customers, and employees to scrutinize AI claims and demand measurable evidence, the author argues that greater accountability is essential to distinguishing genuine innovation from deceptive marketing and investment fraud.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents a critical macro-historical and sociological analysis of the structural transformation of the Canadian state, tracing its mutation from a top-down Euro-Anglo colonial hegemony into a contemporary arena of defensive pluralism. Utilizing the strategic realism of K. Subrahmanyam (1986) alongside the civilizational inversion and "Newly Developing Multi-Religious Country" (NDMC) theories of the author, Sushil Jain (1988–2025), the study investigates the limits of a hyper-litigious, rights-centric multicultural framework

It argues that by dismantling its ancestral Judeo-Christian public architecture to craft a "neutral" public square—culminating in the absolute deregulation of Sunday closing laws under Ontario's New Democratic Party administration in 1992—the state engineered an institutional vacuum. Within this empty space, post-1960s global immigration flows (the 3As: Asia, Africa, Arabia) introduced highly cohesive diasporas operating with long-term strategic intent and community planning, directly contrasting with the host society's self-effacing "humanitarian reflex".

By deploying Arjun Appadurai's global flows framework, the paper illuminates the phenomenon of "Symbolic Inversion" across urban landscapes, education systems, and civic spaces, wherein voluntary guests have emerged as active co-authors of the nation's institutional parameters. This asymmetry has institutionalized an unequal "Emotional Hierarchy," pathologizing native "host grief" and majoritarian cultural bereavement while leaving public spaces vulnerable to imported polarization, separate school board segregation, and communal balkanization.

The paper analyzes Prime Minister Mark Carney's defensive June 2026 "Canadian Covenant" address and the bilateral adoption of the ancient Indian framework of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam as elite, state-level recognitions that a rights-only mosaic is unsustainable. It concludes by validating Jain's visionary 1988 Multicultural Bill of Religious Rights and Responsibilities, asserting that civilizational renewal requires a transition toward a model of strict Civic Realism. True pluralistic survival requires an explicit, binding equilibrium where individual and group rights are structurally tethered to a non-negotiable code of reciprocal national duties.

detail.abstract: Do firms adjust workplace amenities in response to demand shocks? We develop a monopsony framework in which firms jointly determine wages and amenities, and show that the pass-throughs of demand shocks depend crucially on the structure of amenity provision costs. Using Norwegian administrative data that combine matched employer-employee records, firms' cost accounts, and non-pecuniary attributes from job postings, we provide evidence on how firms adjust amenities in response to demand shocks. Exploiting three alternative sources of variation-abrupt value-added changes, public procurement contract wins, and export demand shifts-we document multi-margin adjustments in non-wage compensation, besides wage and employment. We discuss the implications of our findings for the measurement of employer market power.

detail.abstract: AI remuneration may be defended in the name of creators' human rights while leaving creators themselves with little or nothing. This article examines that tension through international human rights law, which protects creators' material interests without equating them with the transferable economic rights under copyright law. It argues that the current EU framework, based on the text and data mining exception and the possibility of licensing following rights reservations, cannot be assumed to protect original creators merely because it allows copyright owners to obtain remuneration. Proposed alternative remuneration mechanisms seek to address this problem by directing economic benefits more closely towards creators. But whether these alternatives genuinely protect creators' material interests is itself a question of human rights law, one that cannot be answered simply by pointing to the benefits they provide. Output-based levies may support the creative community without necessarily protecting the material interests of individual creators whose works were used in AI training; statutory or residual remuneration rights may yield individual payments too small to provide meaningful material protection. Human rights law offers no "magic" remuneration model, but calls for examining whose interests different mechanisms protect, how effectively, and whether individual and collective approaches can complement one another.

detail.abstract: Large language models promise to improve household financial decision-making at scale in domains prone to costly mistakes, yet how their alignment training shapes advice in naturalistic settings remains unclear. I examine this question in health insurance plan choice and retirement portfolio allocationdomains with informative welfare benchmarks-using 112,263 model evaluations across twelve experimental designs, supplemented by administrative data on 15,717 employee insurance choices and a retirement advice experiment with human participants. In a neutral, information-only context, models recommend financially dominated insurance plans in 17.5% of cases, compared with 63.3% of employee choices, and recommend retirement allocations closer than human advice to an industry target-date benchmark. However, disclosures of low risk tolerance, chronic health conditions, or user anxiety shift models toward dominated insurance plans and overly conservative retirement portfolios, eroding much of their baseline advantage and imposing excess insurance costs that fall regressively on lower-income households as a share of earnings. Mechanism experiments and an analysis of 25,950 model explanations indicate that these cues activate protective priorities that models implement heuristically-favoring lower cost sharing in insurance and lower equity exposure in retirement even when doing so conflicts with financial value or an explicit cost-minimization goal. A brief prompt instruction framing the task as economic optimization largely eliminates dominated insurance recommendations while preserving responsiveness to stated risk tolerance. Finally, an evaluation of 1,000 Reddit personal finance posts shows that naturally occurring advice requests frequently elicit protective assessments comparable to those induced by the experimental cues.

detail.abstract: Changes in the Treasury's cash management practices after the COVID pandemic increased the Fed's balance sheet by as much as 2 percentage points of nominal GDP, including the larger buffer required to maintain ample reserve levels. A parsimonious time-series model shows that, once we account for the impact of the Treasury's extraordinary measures during debt-ceiling episodes, the observed changes in the Treasury General Account since COVID are mostly driven by higher target balances. An effective sterilization program by the Fed would require timely and accurate information at high frequencies.

detail.abstract: Intervertebral disc (IVD) degeneration is one of the major concerning spine problems in the world. It is widely graded according to Pfirrmann grading from T2-weighted MRI images. But this assessment remains completely subjective and gives no quantitative values which leads to inter-observer variability. Several approaches have been taken using deep learning and radiomics to address this. However, there are scopes of improvement in incorporating interpretability and automated biomarker computation. In this study, we propose a fully automated pipeline that derives two biologically grounded interpretable imaging biomarkers from routine T2-weighted MRI. These are Nucleus-Annulus T2 Contrast (NATC) and Nucleus T2 Heterogeneity (NTH). Firstly, the MRI segmentation of vertebrae, IVD, and spinal canal was performed by a 3D UNet deep learning architecture using the SPIDER dataset. Then, from the 1502 IVD level observations, both biomarkers were evaluated statistically. They showed a monotonic relation and significant Spearman correlations of -0.435 and -0.406 with Pfirrman grading. The Mann-Whitney U test also showed that they were able to distinguish 90% of the grade pairs. The inter-class correlation coefficientbetween the ground truth and predicted masks for the NATC and NTH were found as 0.876 and 0.874, respectively, which promises the reliability of the fully automated pipeline. The impact of those biomarkers was further investigated for classification of early and advanced degeneration cases. It is observed that incorporation of these biomarkers into the traditional lightweight logistic regression classifier exhibited similar performance compared to a bulky baseline 3D CNN with raw images. Therefore, the two proposed biomarkers demonstrated an interpretable, automated, and clinically deployable alternative to subjective grading and classification based on black-box approaches.
